payload.name: Extract explicit primary goals
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states their number one goal, top priority, or primary aspiration (e.g., 'my number one goal is', 'I most want to'), extract it as a memory candidate during ingestion.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit first-person statements of a primary goal or top priority as high-importance memory candidates (e.g., preference or plan).
If a speaker uses superlative phrasing like 'number one goal', 'top priority', 'most important thing to me', or similar, capture the stated objective without requiring additional confirmation.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: explicit first-person statements of a top priority (e.g., 'number one goal') were skipped during ingestion, causing later recall failure. Mechanism: the construction agent under-extracts superlative goal statements. This skill abstracts that gap by requiring extraction of any explicit primary goal. Applies to future sessions where a speaker states a personal top priority in any domain, but not to implicit or vague aspirations.

payload.name: Extract-Explicit-Importance-Preference-Memory
payload.description: When a user explicitly says something is important, valued, or a priority, apply during construction extraction or update to create or update a preference memory capturing that claim even if the same message also describes an event or action.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit stated value or importance (e.g., 'X is really important to me', 'I value Y'), extract it as a separate preference memory for the speaker, in addition to any event or action memory from the same message.

During update or enrichment, when a later message restates or reinforces such an explicit importance, add it to the existing memory if absent; do not let it be absorbed into an event narrative where it becomes implicit.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: the extraction candidate preserved the routine event but dropped the speaker's explicit statement that something is important to them, so the memory could not answer why the routine happened. The reusable mechanism is treating explicit importance/value statements as secondary to an event. This skill applies to future construction passes where a message declares a value or priority; it should persist that claim as a preference memory, separate from any event narrative. It does not apply to preferences that are only inferred, not explicitly stated.

payload.name: Extract reminder-linked personal values
payload.description: When a user mentions an object, image, quote, or practice as a reminder of a personal value, goal, or identity, extract that value as a preference or state memory.
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker says they have or use something (e.g., a painting, photo, quote, ritual) to remind them to uphold a specific value or goal, create a memory of that value/goal as a preference or state.
Store the underlying value or aspiration (e.g., 'be a leader'), not just the fact of owning the object.
If a memory for the same value already exists, perform an UPDATE or MERGE instead of creating a duplicate.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip self-descriptive statements where a user mentions a physical object or symbol as a reminder of a personal value or goal, leaving the underlying aspiration unrecorded. This skill guides extraction of such statements into durable preference/state memories, regardless of the conversational topic or object involved. It should be applied whenever a speaker explicitly links an object or ritual to a value they strive to uphold; it is not intended for mere object ownership statements or for values attributed to other people.

payload.name: Extract each explicitly stated goal as a distinct memory
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states multiple goals, priorities, or aspirations in one message or across a conversation, extract each distinct goal as its own candidate memory instead of merging or omitting one.
content: During extraction, create a separate candidate memory for each explicitly stated goal or aspiration (e.g., 'my goal is', 'I want to', 'number one goal', 'also want'), even when multiple appear in the same message or turn.
Do not merge multiple distinct goals into one broader memory; keep each goal independently so that downstream reference claims can be matched.

Treat emphatic or superlative goal statements ('my number one goal', 'most important goal') as ordinary explicit goals and extract them even if another goal was already captured from an earlier exchange.

candidates.solves: Extraction may drop or merge one explicitly stated goal when a message contains multiple goals, especially a goal introduced as "number one" alongside other goals. The rule to extract each distinct goal as its own memory candidate is a valid general remedy for any multi-goal statement. It applies to future conversations where a speaker lists multiple goals, aspirations, or priorities in one message or across turns.

payload.name: preserve-confirmed-ordinals-when-extracting-events
payload.description: When extracting an event or profile memory from dialogue, include an ordinal qualifier (first, second, third) and the item type whenever the speaker explicitly confirms them.
content: During extraction, treat an explicitly confirmed ordinal as a core fact. If the speaker answers a yes/no ordinal question with confirmation, record 'third [item]' in the candidate content.
Do not add an ordinal when it is only a guess or not directly confirmed; record only explicitly stated attributes.
Include the item type named in the original question along with the ordinal and any thematic details.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often retain thematic detail but drop explicitly confirmed ordinal identifiers, making later queries about 'third X' unanswerable. This rule applies whenever a user confirms an ordinal in conversation and a memory is extracted; it does not apply to unconfirmed guesses or implied numbers.

payload.name: Extract explicit confidence and motivation strategies as preferences
payload.description: When a person explicitly states how they stay confident, motivated, or cope with challenges in work/business, extract those stated strategies as preference candidates during construction.
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker explicitly describes recurring strategies for staying confident, motivated, or handling setbacks (e.g., 'I stay motivated by...', 'It helps to have...', 'I focus on...'), create one preference candidate for each distinct strategy. Do not skip these statements as conversational filler, because they are durable facts about the speaker.

candidates.solves: Construction ingestion can silently drop explicit statements about how a person stays confident, motivated, or handles setbacks, especially when they appear inside supportive advice exchanges. This rule ensures such self-disclosed strategies are extracted as preference memories so later questions about mindset can be answered; it applies to explicit 'I stay motivated/cope by...' statements but not to implied strategies or one-off actions.

payload.name: Extract spoken descriptions of shared photos
payload.description: When a user shares a photo in a message and immediately adds adjectives describing the subject, extract a memory of that description during construction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a message includes a photo and an accompanying descriptive phrase (e.g., superlatives or adjectives) that refers to a person, pet, object, or event already discussed, create a memory candidate for the speaker's description. Use the existing memory type that fits (e.g., preference or event), include the described subject and the quoted phrase, and do not skip it because the photo itself contributes no text.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because descriptive statements attached to image shares were not extracted into candidates, causing the referenced fact to be absent from memory. The reusable mechanism is that evaluative phrases following a photo often describe an object already mentioned in the conversation. Future inputs with photo-sharing and short descriptive wording in the same message should trigger extraction rather than being skipped.

payload.name: capture-explicit-sharing-events
payload.description: When a user explicitly shares or references a picture, photo, or artifact with descriptive details, extract the sharing event itself, not just the underlying object's attributes.
content: If a message contains an explicit sharing reference (e.g., 'This is my...', 'Here is...', 'That picture is...'), create an event memory that records the act of sharing, the item shared, and any creator/source details from the same message.
When extracting from such a message, do not only store ownership or static attributes; include the sharing action so that questions about what was shared can be answered.
If an existing memory already covers the object's attributes, still add or merge the sharing event to preserve the action.

candidates.solves: When a user explicitly shares or references a picture, photo, or artifact in a message, the extraction stage sometimes records only the object's attributes (e.g., ownership) and omits the fact that the user shared it. This causes later questions about the shared item to fail. The rule abstracts the need to capture the act of sharing/referencing as part of the durable memory, along with any descriptive details, applicable to any conversation where a user presents an item and gives its origin or description.

payload.name: Preserve Stated Social Relationships from Team Activities
payload.description: When extracting or updating memories from statements about team/group activities, create a separate relationship memory for the stated companions and do not let event updates erase it.
content: During extraction, if a statement explicitly mentions the person acting with a team, group, or companions (e.g., 'with my team', 'together with friends'), add a relationship memory capturing that the person has those teammates/companions, in addition to any event memory.
During CRUD, when updating or enriching an event memory, preserve any stated team/group/companion relationship unless new evidence explicitly contradicts it.
Before finalizing a memory change, check that relationship implications from source messages are represented as relationship memories, not only embedded in event descriptions.

candidates.solves: A social fact such as having teammates or friends was only embedded in an event memory and disappeared when the event was later rewritten. The fix is to extract stated team/group/companion relationships as separate relationship memories and keep them intact during event updates. This applies whenever a speaker mentions participating with a team, group, or other people, but not when no social relationship is explicitly stated.

payload.name: Extract support-object relationship memories
payload.description: When a user explicitly says an object, pet, or item helps them focus, calms them, comforts them, or brings them joy, use a relationship memory even if the item is a toy or stuffed animal.
content: Use a relationship memory when the user explicitly says an object, pet, or item helps them stay focused, calms them, comforts them, or brings them joy; this includes stuffed animals and other toys.
During extraction, always create a candidate for such explicit benefit statements instead of dismissing them as small talk or non-factual.
During CRUD, add or merge this relationship memory with the item's identifying details (e.g., name, type) and attach the stated benefit.

candidates.solves: Extraction under-generates when users explicitly state an object or pet provides emotional or functional support (focus, joy, calm), so the relationship is never persisted. A reusable rule should record such explicit benefit statements as relationship memories, including for stuffed animals and toys, while excluding generic compliments or statements without a named item.

payload.name: Carry forward established location context during extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event from a later message, check earlier session messages for a location already established for the same trip or ongoing context and include it in the candidate memory if the event is clearly tied to that context.
content: Before finalizing an event candidate, scan earlier messages in the same session for a location associated with the same trip or ongoing context.
If the current message describes an activity clearly connected to that established context without repeating the location, include that location in the memory content.
Do not infer a location when the event is not explicitly connected to a prior place or when the context indicates a different location.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an event extracted from a later message omitted the location already established earlier in the same session, so the memory could not answer a later question about where the event happened. The reusable mechanism is that construction extraction must carry forward relevant location context from prior turns when the current event is clearly tied to that context, instead of only using words in the immediate message. This applies to any future session where an activity is mentioned without repeating a previously stated place.

payload.name: Resolve relative time in extracted events
payload.description: When extracting an event memory and the source message contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week', 'two days ago'), use the message/session timestamp to compute the absolute date and include it in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if the source text contains a relative temporal phrase such as 'a year ago', 'last week', 'two days ago', or 'yesterday', resolve it to a concrete date or year using the message's occurred_at timestamp and store that resolved value as part of the memory content.
If the exact date cannot be determined, store the closest approximate absolute value (e.g., year) and do not drop the temporal information entirely.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops relative time expressions ('a year ago', 'last week') when creating memories, leaving event timing unknown. This Skill provides a rule to resolve such expressions using the message timestamp and include the absolute date in the memory, applicable to any event/purchase/occurrence extraction.

payload.name: Extract dated events from emotional narratives
payload.description: When a user mentions a personal event with an explicit year or date inside emotional or photo-sharing language, use it to create an event memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a user explicitly mentions a personal event (e.g., wedding, birth, move, graduation) with an explicit year or date, create an event memory with the event type and that date even if the surrounding message is emotional, nostalgic, or describes photos.
Do not treat emotional or reflective framing as a reason to skip extraction; explicit dated facts remain durable memories regardless of tone.
When the date is relative (e.g., 'two years ago'), resolve it from the message/session timestamp before creating the event memory.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because a dated personal event embedded in nostalgic photo-sharing language produced no extraction candidates. The abstract mechanism is that explicit event dates are skipped when the utterance is emotionally framed. This applies to any future message where a user states a personal event with a year or date amid reflective, grief-related, or memory-sharing wording, and it should trigger creation of an event memory with that date.

payload.name: ExtractUserPastEventWithTime
payload.description: When a user discloses a past personal action with a relative time reference (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday'), extract an event memory candidate during ingestion.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit user statements about their own past actions (e.g., 'I made', 'I visited') as event memory candidates, even if they appear inside casual conversation or a question.

Resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday') against the message/session timestamp and store the resolved date in the event memory; include the action and key object in the content.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because an obvious user-stated past event (making a dessert) was not extracted as a memory, leaving the claim missing. The underlying mechanism is the extraction stage overlooking self-reported past actions with relative time references. This skill generalizes to any future session where a user mentions a past action they performed with a time expression, ensuring it becomes an event memory. It does not apply to actions by others, hypotheticals, or future plans.

payload.name: Resolve relative event dates during extraction
payload.description: Use when extracting event memories from a message that contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'on Friday', 'last week', 'yesterday') and the message/session timestamp can resolve it to an absolute date.
content: During extraction, resolve relative temporal expressions (e.g., 'on Friday', 'last week') against the message/session timestamp and record the resolved absolute date for the event occurrence.

When a message contains both an event occurrence date and a future plan/start date, keep them distinct: store the occurrence date as the event's date and include the future start as additional context rather than using it as the event date.
Include explicit date anchors in candidate memory content so downstream questions about when an event happened can be answered from memory alone.

candidates.solves: When a message reports an event with a relative day (e.g., 'on Friday') and also mentions a future milestone (e.g., 'next month'), extraction may drop the event date and store only the future start, making the exact occurrence date unanswerable. This Skill enforces resolving relative dates against the message timestamp and preserving the occurrence date separately from any later plan, so future 'when did X happen?' questions can be answered from memory. It applies to event extraction from messages with a usable timestamp, not to planning statements without an occurrence date.

payload.name: Resolve relative dates and preserve first-time markers in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting event memories, if the source message uses a relative time (yesterday, last week, today) or a first/ordinal marker, resolve the exact date from the message/session timestamp and keep the marker in the candidate content.
content: Scan each source message for relative time expressions ('yesterday', 'last week', 'today') and resolve them to concrete dates using the message/session timestamp; store the resolved date instead of vague phrasing like 'recently'.
If the message includes a first-time or ordinal marker ('for the first time', 'first', 'once'), preserve that qualifier in the extracted event content because it is a durable, queryable fact.

candidates.solves: Extraction often loses explicit event facts by paraphrasing relative dates as vague terms (e.g., 'recently') and dropping 'first time' qualifiers, making later date or ordinal questions unanswerable. This rule applies whenever a message describes an event relative to its timestamp or marks an occurrence as first, and instructs extraction to resolve and preserve those details.

payload.name: Preserve explicit timing in extracted event memories
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message that includes an explicit time phrase like 'a year ago', 'last week', or 'in 2020', include that timing in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a source message states a time for an event (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week', 'in 2020'), record that temporal detail in the memory content rather than omitting it while keeping entities and locations.

Resolve relative time expressions against the session/message timestamp when needed, but keep the explicit temporal anchor or its resolved value in the memory so the event's timing remains answerable.
Apply this to all event memories such as purchases, acquisitions, or occurrences whenever the timing is explicitly mentioned.

candidates.solves: When constructing an event memory, explicit temporal expressions such as 'a year ago', 'last week', or 'in 2020' are sometimes dropped while entities and locations are kept, making time-based questions unanswerable. This skill ensures such timing details are preserved or resolved in extracted event memories whenever the source states them.

payload.name: Extract_past_events_with_relative_time
payload.description: When a message includes a first-person past event with a relative time expression (last Friday, yesterday, etc.), extract it as its own event memory during construction, resolving the date from the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a first-person past activity or experience with a relative time expression (e.g., "last Friday", "yesterday", "last week"), create a separate extraction candidate with memory_kind "event" for it, even if the message's main topic is something else (like encouragement or advice).

Resolve the relative time phrase using the message's occurred_at timestamp to produce the concrete date, and include the activity, subject, and any companions mentioned (e.g., "with a group of friends"). Do not merge this event into a memory about the speaker's attitude or relationship; multiple candidates from one message are allowed.

candidates.solves: Construction agents often drop a speaker's passing past event if the message focuses on another topic, especially with relative time phrases. This Skill triggers on first-person past activities with relative time references (last Friday, yesterday), requiring a separate event candidate with date resolved from the message timestamp. Not for hypothetical plans, general statements, or third-person reports.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeEventTimesInMemory
payload.description: When constructing memories from user statements that include relative time cues for an action (e.g., 'recently', 'last week', 'just'), resolve the absolute date from the message timestamp and store the action as an event with its date.
content: If a message contains a relative time expression (recently, last week, this month, just, etc.) tied to a stated action, resolve the absolute date using the message/session timestamp and include both the action verb and that date in the memory content.
Prefer creating or updating an event-kind memory for such time-bound actions; do not merge them into a general profile with present-tense wording that erases the date.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an extraction candidate lost the temporal anchor of a dated action ('recently joined...' on 4 Nov 2023) by folding it into a generic profile ('participates') without the date. The abstract failure is the loss of event timing when converting relative-time statements into memory. This Skill applies to any construction session where a user message describes a time-bound action with relative time wording, ensuring the action verb and absolute date are preserved in memory content.

payload.name: Resolve relative time in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory and the source message contains a relative time phrase such as 'last week', 'yesterday', or 'a few days ago', use this Skill to convert that phrase to an absolute date range based on the message/session timestamp.
content: During extraction of an event memory, when the source message contains a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), resolve that phrase against the message/session timestamp and set world_start (and world_end when the phrase implies a range) to the implied date range, not the message date. If exact day is unknown, encode the earliest and latest plausible dates from the relative phrase; do not let the message date become the event time.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops relative time references ('last week', 'yesterday') from event memories, using the message date as the event start and losing true occurrence time. This Skill makes extraction resolve such phrases against the message/session timestamp and store the implied date range in world_start/world_end. It applies to future event extraction with relative timing; it does not apply to profile/preference extraction or to CRUD updates not involving temporal resolution.

payload.name: Resolve-relative-time-in-extraction
payload.description: When extracting candidate memories from a message, if the message contains a relative time expression ('last year', 'yesterday', 'last week') and the message timestamp is available, resolve it to an absolute date and include it in the candidate before CRUD.
content: During extraction, for every statement about a past event that includes a relative time reference, convert that reference to an absolute date using the message's timestamp (e.g., 'last year' on 1 Dec 2023 -> 2022).
Create an 'event' memory candidate for such past occurrences even if the date is only implicit, and include the resolved date in the memory content.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because a past event described only as 'last year' was not extracted, so no event memory was created. This is a recurring failure for relative time expressions, which are easy to skip when no explicit date appears. This Skill applies whenever a message with a timestamp contains a relative time phrase and a past event should be stored; it does not apply to messages without timestamps or to general statements lacking a time reference.

payload.name: Preserve-cumulative-event-counts
payload.description: When a message reports a new event in a countable series (e.g., second, fourth, final win/achievement), add a distinct event memory instead of updating or overwriting an earlier event memory.
content: During candidate extraction, when a message describes another occurrence in an ongoing countable series for the same person (e.g., a second, fourth, or final tournament win), extract it as a new event candidate; do not treat it as an update to an earlier event memory just because it is more recent.

During CRUD decisions, preserve prior discrete event memories when adding a new series occurrence; only UPDATE or ENRICH a memory when the new content genuinely refines that same occurrence, never when it describes a different instance. If the session implies a cumulative total, create or update a separate concise summary memory (e.g., 'has won N tournaments') without deleting individual event records.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an UPDATE replaced Nate's first tournament win with his fourth, losing the cumulative count. Abstract mechanism: a new occurrence in a countable series was treated as a replacement for an older occurrence. Applies whenever future sessions mention sequential achievements/events (wins, awards, milestones) and counts must be preserved. Boundary: does not apply to enriching the same single event with additional details.

payload.name: Preserve distinct event instances on update
payload.description: When updating a memory, if the new message describes a different occurrence of a similar event (different ordinal, time, or instance), do not overwrite the existing memory; add a new memory while preserving the old.
content: During CRUD update, before replacing an existing memory, check whether the incoming event is the same instance or a new instance of a repeated event type.
If the new event has a different ordinal (first, second, fourth, etc.), different date/time, or otherwise different occurrence context, treat it as a separate event.
Preserve the existing memory unchanged and ADD a new memory for the new event instance. Do not merge distinct instances into one memory by overwriting the old content.
Only overwrite or enrich an existing memory when the new information clearly refers to the exact same event instance already recorded.

candidates.solves: When new evidence describes another occurrence of a repeated event type (e.g., first vs. fourth win), the construction agent may overwrite an older memory with the later occurrence, erasing a question-answerable fact. This rule distinguishes event instances by ordinal, time, or context and preserves earlier memories by adding separate memories for new instances. It applies to any recurring event domain (tournaments, trips, jobs) during CRUD updates, not to enriching the same event instance.

payload.name: Preserve existing facts during memory updates
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing memory, keep all previously recorded facts that are not contradicted by new evidence; add new details instead of replacing the entire content.
content: Before applying UPDATE or MERGE to an existing memory, compare the proposed new content with the existing memory content.

Retain every existing fact that remains true and is not explicitly contradicted by the new message; if new evidence adds context or corrects a detail, revise only the affected portion and keep the rest.

If the new information describes a different aspect or event, prefer ADDing a new memory or enriching with an additional sentence; do not rewrite the memory so that previously supported claims disappear.
When an update would remove an earlier explicit statement, treat it as suspect and instead produce content that includes both the old and new facts.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was an UPDATE that rewrote a memory's content based on a later message and erased a previously captured fact that the later message did not contradict. This abstract failure occurs whenever a construction agent treats a later message as a replacement for the whole memory instead of as incremental enrichment. The rule applies to future UPDATE/MERGE decisions on any topic: preserve all non-contradicted existing facts, add new details, and only drop information explicitly invalidated by the new evidence.

payload.name: Preserve existing facts when updating memories
payload.description: When a new message describes a different event or topic than an existing memory, keep the original content and ADD or MERGE rather than overwriting.
content: Before updating an existing memory, compare the new message's event/topic with the stored memory's event/topic.
If they differ, do not replace the existing memory; create a new memory for the new facts or merge by appending while retaining the original content.
Preserve previously stored durable facts unless the new message explicitly contradicts them.

candidates.solves: A later construction update can overwrite a correctly stored memory with unrelated facts from a new message, deleting previously captured durable claims. The rule separates distinct events/topics: before replacing an existing memory, check whether the new facts concern the same event/topic; if not, add a separate memory or merge while preserving original content. It does not apply when the new message directly contradicts the old memory, in which case updating is appropriate.

payload.name: PreservePriorFactsOnMemoryUpdate
payload.description: When updating an existing memory with new details about the same subject, preserve previously stored facts unless directly contradicted by the new evidence.
content: During UPDATE operations on an existing memory, merge the new information into the existing content instead of replacing the whole memory. Keep all prior facts that are not explicitly contradicted by the new message. If a fact is genuinely contradicted, remove only that fact and update it with the corrected value; retain all other existing facts.

candidates.solves: When an UPDATE rewrites an existing memory using only the newest message's details, earlier true facts about the same subject can be silently dropped. The reusable rule is to treat memory updates as merges: preserve prior facts unless directly contradicted by new evidence, and replace or remove only the superseded portion. This applies whenever a later message enriches or corrects an already-stored profile, preference, or entity memory.

payload.name: Preserve event date during enrichment updates
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing event memory with new information, if the new message does not explicitly restate or change the event date, keep the original world_start unchanged.
content: Before applying an UPDATE/MERGE to an event memory, check whether the triggering message explicitly provides a new date for the same event.
If the new message only adds related context or a separate event, do not change the original world_start; preserve the date already supported by earlier evidence.
When merging multiple events into one memory, retain each event's original date rather than assigning the latest message time to all contained events.

candidates.solves: When a later message enriches an existing event memory but does not explicitly change the event's date, the Construction Agent must not overwrite the original world_start with the later message timestamp. The diagnosed failure changed an originally correct launch date during an unrelated enrichment update, so future updates should preserve the existing temporal anchor unless the new evidence explicitly revises it.

payload.name: Fact-preserving merge for new activity candidates
payload.description: When a construction decision would MERGE a candidate event into an existing memory and the candidate introduces a new activity, class, course, or group, use fact-preserving merge that keeps every distinct fact from both sides.
content: During the decision stage, before applying MERGE to a candidate, compare the candidate's content against the proposed merged content. If any distinct fact from the candidate (such as enrolling in a class, course, workshop, or group) is absent from the merged result, preserve it: either append that fact explicitly to the merged memory or ADD the candidate as a separate memory.

When a MERGE changes an existing memory's object/activity label to the candidate's new label, verify the new activity itself appears in the resulting content. Changing only the label while keeping old details is not enough and loses the candidate fact.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions that MERGE a candidate describing a new event or activity into an existing memory can silently drop the candidate's core fact, as happened when an agility-class candidate was merged into a hiking/dog-park memory and the class was absent from the merged content. The abstract failure is merging without fact preservation. This rule applies whenever a future candidate introduces a distinct event/activity/class/course/group and the decision is to merge it with a broader existing memory; it ensures no durable fact is lost.

payload.name: Preserve distinct event facts during updates
payload.description: When a later user message describes an event or plan different from the primary activity in an existing memory, do not overwrite the memory's object_text or core content; create a new memory or append while preserving the old fact.
content: When an incoming message mentions a new event or plan for a subject, check whether an existing event memory already records a different primary activity. If the activities are distinct, do not overwrite the memory's object_text or remove its core content; instead create a new event/plan memory or append the new fact while preserving the old one.

During candidate extraction, treat each explicitly distinct activity or plan as its own event candidate with its own timing and source, even when the same subject already appears in earlier memories; do not collapse them into a single mutable summary.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was an UPDATE that replaced a memory's object_text ('agility classes') with a later planned activity ('stroll'), erasing a previously extracted fact. The abstract failure mechanism is conflating a newly mentioned distinct activity with an existing memory and letting the update overwrite the memory's central topic. The rule applies whenever a later message describes a different event or plan for a subject that already has a memory, preserving durable facts across construction.

payload.name: Preserve candidate facts when merging memories
payload.description: When a construction MERGE combines a new candidate with an existing memory, use the merged content to retain all distinct facts from the candidate, such as donation beneficiaries or organizations.
content: During construction CRUD, when applying a MERGE, compare candidate content with the existing memory and ensure every discrete factual assertion from the candidate appears in the new version.

If the candidate names a donation recipient, cause, organization, or similar affiliation, keep that fact in the merged memory; if the existing memory cannot hold it without losing other key facts, create or update a separate memory for that fact instead of dropping it.

candidates.solves: Construction MERGE decisions sometimes collapse a candidate into a related existing memory and accidentally drop a discrete fact that was present in the candidate (here, the donation recipient). Future questions may ask about that dropped fact, so the merged memory must preserve every distinct fact from the candidate. This applies only to CRUD merge operations on construction candidates, not to retrieval or answer generation, and does not require retaining non-factual wording or irrelevant details.

payload.name: Preserve distinct events during memory update
payload.description: When updating an existing event memory, apply this if the new message describes a different activity, time, or plan than the stored event, to avoid overwriting unrelated information.
content: Before applying an UPDATE to an existing event memory, compare the new message's activity, time, and subject with the stored content. If they describe different events, do not replace the stored content.

If the new information is a separate event, either create a new memory for it or merge it into the existing memory as additional context while preserving all previously recorded planned or occurred events.
When merging multiple events into one memory, keep each event's time and subject explicit so future retrieval can still find every relevant plan.

candidates.solves: Construction failed when a later UPDATE overwrote an existing planned event with a new, unrelated event, deleting the earlier fact. The abstract mechanism is treating any new event as a replacement of the target memory rather than recognizing it as a separate event. A rule that requires checking subject, time, and activity before UPDATE preserves coexisting events and transfers to any domain with multiple plans or activities for the same person or group.

payload.name: Preserve prior facts when updating memories
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with new information, preserve all previously stored facts unless directly contradicted or superseded; if new details describe a separate event, keep both instead of overwriting.
content: Before applying UPDATE or MERGE, compare new evidence against existing memory content and retain every old fact that is not explicitly contradicted or superseded by the new message.
If the new information describes a different event, time period, or state of the world, do not overwrite older content; append it or create a separate memory so earlier facts remain available.
When changing world_start or state, still keep durable background facts that remain true, such as preferences, ongoing activities, and long-term care routines.

candidates.solves: When a new event or state is added to an existing memory, the update should not replace the entire memory and drop previously stored facts. The diagnosed failure occurred because an UPDATE to a memory about a beach trip replaced the content with a later knee-injury event, losing the beach fact. This rule abstracts that mechanism: during UPDATE/MERGE, preserve non-contradicted facts or split into separate memories. It applies to any future session where new evidence is recorded against an existing memory that contains multiple independent facts.

payload.name: Preserve unrelated plans during memory updates
payload.description: When updating a memory, if the incoming message introduces a different plan or event for the same subject, add a new memory instead of overwriting the existing one.
content: Before executing an UPDATE on an existing memory, compare the new evidence with the memory's current content. If they describe different plans, projects, events, or topics, do not overwrite the old memory; ADD a new memory for the new information and leave the existing memory unchanged.
When extracting candidates, treat distinct plans or events for the same subject as separate memories unless new evidence explicitly supersedes or corrects the earlier plan.
If a message only adds details to an existing plan, UPDATE or enrich that memory; if it introduces an unrelated activity, preserve the original and create a separate entry.

candidates.solves: A construction UPDATE can replace a prior correct memory with unrelated content when a later message mentions a different plan by the same person. This rule prevents loss of earlier evidence by requiring the agent to verify topical alignment before UPDATE and to ADD new distinct plans separately. Applies to any future update where new and old memory are not revisions of the same claim.

payload.name: Preserve prior facts when updating event memories
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing event memory with details from a later message, preserve all still-valid previously stored facts and avoid replacing the whole content with only the new activity.
content: During UPDATE or MERGE on an existing event memory, treat the existing content as preserved by default: keep every fact that remains true; never overwrite the entire content with only the new message's details.

When a later message describes a different activity or event than the memory currently stores, do not replace object_text/content with the new topic. Update only genuinely changed fields, or ADD a separate memory for the new event, so earlier facts remain retrievable.

candidates.solves: Construction agents can destroy previously captured facts when a later message triggers an UPDATE that rewrites an existing event memory with new activity details, making earlier claims unanswerable. This skill applies whenever one memory is updated or enriched from a new message; it requires preserving all still-valid existing facts and narrowing edits to genuinely changed fields, creating a new memory when the new event is distinct.

payload.name: Preserve old facts when updating an event memory
payload.description: When updating an existing event or state memory with facts from a new message, check whether the update would drop or overwrite previously stored durable facts from the same subject that are not contradicted or subsumed by the new content; preserve them by merging or splitting instead of replacing.
content: During the update stage, before applying an UPDATE, compare the target memory's current content with the new candidate facts from the triggering message.

If the new facts describe different events, states, preferences, or relationships than the old content and do not contradict or fully supersede it, do not overwrite the existing memory. Keep the old memory unchanged and add a separate new memory for the new facts, or merge them into a combined content that retains all distinct durable claims.

When a new message mentions an activity or emotion that elaborates on an existing memory's topic without invalidating the old statement, preserve the original claim and its reason/cause; do not let a newer activity replace an older fact merely because it is newer.

After any UPDATE or enrichment, verify that every true claim from the referenced prior memory version remains present in the resulting memory or another memory; if a previously stored fact disappears, restore it.

candidates.solves: When updating an existing memory from a new message, the agent may overwrite old durable facts. This Skill applies to UPDATE operations where new content does not contradict or subsume old content and the old facts remain true; preserve them by merging or splitting instead of replacing. It does not apply to DELETEs, corrections, or direct contradictions.

payload.name: Preserve specific facts when updating memories
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing memory with new information, retain all previously recorded specific facts that are not explicitly contradicted; merge rather than replace.
content: Before applying an UPDATE or enrichment to an existing memory, compare the existing content against new evidence and list existing factual details (e.g., specific type, exact date, duration) that are not contradicted; these must be kept.

When new information adds context but does not explicitly contradict an existing fact, preserve the original specific detail and add the new detail as supplemental, rather than overwriting the original with a paraphrase or inference.

Only change world_start or other temporal fields when new evidence explicitly revises the event date; resolve relative expressions like 'last week' from the message timestamp and match them to the existing timeframe.

candidates.solves: Updates to existing event memories often replace precise details (specific injury type, exact date) with broader paraphrases or inferred causes from later messages, losing answerable facts. This skill instructs construction agents to preserve uncontradicted specific facts when enriching, keeping event content and timing faithful to all evidence. Applies whenever a later message adds context to a previously stored event without explicitly negating earlier details.

payload.name: Preserve distinct events during memory updates
payload.description: When a later message describes an event that differs from an existing memory's date, outcome, or completion status, do not overwrite the existing event memory; keep it and add a separate memory for the new event.
content: Before updating an existing event memory, compare the new message with the stored content: if the event date, completion status, or core facts differ, the new message describes a distinct event. Do not overwrite the original memory; preserve it and create a separate memory for the new event if it is durable.
When extracting candidates, treat events with different dates or different outcomes as separate memories, even if they share the same subject and topic.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an UPDATE overwrote a correct earlier event memory with a different later event, losing the original completion date and status. The abstract failure is conflating two distinct events during update/extraction by replacing rather than preserving older facts. This rule applies when a construction agent processes messages that reference the same subject but different temporal or outcome details; it guides the agent to keep distinct events separate instead of destructive overwrite.

payload.name: Preserve distinct events during memory updates
payload.description: When a new message describes an event related but temporally distinct from an existing memory, use ADD for the new event instead of UPDATE overwriting the old one.
content: When extracting a new event that is temporally distinct from an existing memory about the same subject, do not UPDATE the old memory's content or world_start to match the new event; instead ADD a new memory for the new event and leave the existing memory unchanged.

candidates.solves: Construction failures occur when an existing memory about an earlier event is overwritten by a later, distinct event during UPDATE, losing the original date and details. This rule prevents that by requiring temporally distinct events to be stored as separate memories rather than merging them into one. It applies to any subject with multiple related events at different times.

payload.name: Preserve existing dates when enriching memories
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with new information, keep all original dates and factual details; do not let a new date replace or obscure the old one.
content: During UPDATE/MERGE of an existing memory, retain all original temporal details (explicit dates, relative times, world_start/world_end) in the updated memory; do not omit or overwrite them when adding new facts.
If the update adds a new dated event to the same memory, record both dates explicitly in the content unless one event genuinely supersedes the other.
Before finalizing an update, verify that every key fact and date from the prior memory version is still present and unambiguous in the new version.

candidates.solves: When enriching an existing memory with a new event or fact, update/merge operations can drop or obscure the original event's date, causing later questions about the earlier event to be only partially answerable. This rule preserves all existing temporal anchors and factual details during any UPDATE/MERGE that adds new information, so future retrieval can still resolve the original event's date. It applies whenever a memory is extended with a later event, but not when new information intentionally corrects or supersedes an old date.

payload.name: Preserve previous item when updating with a new instance
payload.description: When constructing memories and an existing memory stores one item (e.g., a book) but a later message mentions a different item in the same category, use this Skill before choosing UPDATE.
content: During extraction, when a message names a new item in a category (book, movie, game, hobby) and an existing memory already names a different item, emit the new item as an ADD candidate, not as an UPDATE/correction of the existing one, unless the speaker explicitly retracts or contradicts the earlier item.

During CRUD, if an existing 'currently reading/watching/using' memory describes a different item, preserve that old memory (close its world_end or keep it as a past event) and ADD the new item as a separate memory; use update_type correction only when the old memory is factually wrong.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: a new book mention was treated as a correction, so an UPDATE overwrote an old reading memory. The abstract failure is confusing an additional instance with a correction; when a new item in a category already has a stored item, preserve the prior fact and add the new item separately. Applies to multi-item categories (books, movies, hobbies); not when the speaker explicitly retracts or corrects the old fact.

payload.name: Preserve candidate facts during memory merge
payload.description: When merging a memory candidate into an existing memory, use this if the candidate contains a fact absent from the target; ensure the merged version retains the candidate's full set of facts, including ongoing plans.
content: Before MERGE, compare the candidate content against the target memory content. Any discrete fact present in the candidate but not in the target must appear in the merged content, even if the target is an event and the candidate is a plan.

When the candidate's memory kind differs from the target's (e.g., merging a plan into an event), treat the candidate's predicate as a durable fact that must survive the merge; do not replace content with a summary that omits it.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions sometimes merge a candidate into an existing memory and the merged text drops facts that were only in the candidate, especially when the candidate is a different memory kind (e.g., a plan) and the target is an event. This leads to unsupported future answers. The rule applies to any future merge where candidate and target overlap topically but the candidate introduces a new predicate, such as an ongoing donation, commitment, or other persistent fact; the merged memory must preserve that fact explicitly.

payload.name: Preserve Past Event Facts During Update
payload.description: When updating an existing past event memory and the new message introduces a future plan or separate event involving the same subject, use ADD for the new plan/event and do not change the existing memory's kind, world_start, or original content.
content: Before UPDATE, check whether the incoming information describes a different time period or event kind than the existing memory's stored timeframe. If so, do not overwrite the existing event's memory_kind, world_start/world_end, or core facts; create a new memory instead.

When a message mentions a future plan (e.g., 'next month') and the retrieved memory is a completed past event, keep the past event unchanged and ADD a separate `plan` memory for the future item with its own date.

If an UPDATE is genuinely enriching the same event, preserve the original event's date and memory_kind and only append compatible details; never promote an event to a plan or shift its start date to match a new plan.

candidates.solves: Construction updates often corrupt correct past-event memories when later messages introduce a related future plan or separate event. This Skill ensures distinct facts are kept as distinct memories, preventing loss of date ranges and event kind, and applies to any subject where a future plan or separate event is mentioned after a past event has been stored.

payload.name: Preserve original event facts on related updates
payload.description: When updating an existing event memory and the incoming message describes a later development of the same project, work, or task, preserve the original achievement facts by adding a new memory or limiting the update to changed fields.
content: If a new message reports a later development of an already recorded event (e.g., showing, publishing, or presenting completed work), do not replace the original event content with the new development.
Prefer ADD a separate event memory for the later development, or UPDATE only non-core fields while retaining the original completion date, action, and outcome.
During extraction, when the same subject/work appears in a later message, extract the new information as a candidate for a new event unless the message explicitly revises the earlier fact.

candidates.solves: When a later message describes a new development of a work whose original completion was already stored, the construction agent sometimes overwrites the older event memory, erasing original achievement facts. The reusable rule is to treat later related developments as additive or separate memories, preserving completion and date. This applies whenever a new message references a previously recorded project, task, or creation.

payload.name: Maintain cumulative counts for repeated events
payload.description: Apply when extracting or updating memories and a new message describes another occurrence of an event type already recorded for the same subject, especially wording like 'another', 'again', or 'second time'; use it to store the cumulative occurrence count.
content: When a message describes another occurrence of a countable event already recorded for the same subject, extract a memory that states the cumulative total (e.g., 'second rejection', 'two rejections') rather than only recording the new isolated instance.

Before ADDing a repeated event, search the existing memory pool for prior events of the same subject and event type; if found, create or update an aggregate memory with the total count and mention the prior occurrence dates, while keeping individual event memories intact.

candidates.solves: The construction agent stored each repeated rejection as an isolated event without an explicit total, so a later question asking how many times the event occurred could not be answered from memory. The reusable mechanism is that repeated countable events for the same subject need an explicit cumulative count maintained as new occurrences arrive, not just separate event records. This applies to any future conversation where the same type of countable event recurs (rejections, wins, submissions, purchases) and a count query may follow.

payload.name: Preserve-all-explicitly-enumerated-components
payload.description: When extracting or updating memory from a message that explicitly lists multiple distinct qualities, reasons, or preferences, use this to ensure every listed component is preserved and none is omitted during summarization.
content: During extraction, if the source message explicitly enumerates multiple distinct traits, reasons, or preferences, write the candidate to include every enumerated component; do not condense by dropping any item.

Before committing a memory, compare its content against the source message's list and verify that each explicitly stated component is represented, adding any missing item to the memory content or update.

candidates.solves: Lossy paraphrasing during extraction omits one component when a source explicitly lists multiple qualities. A preserve-every-listed-item rule fixes this and applies to any future multi-item preference, reason, or attribute statement, without inventing unstated details.

payload.name: Cross-check multi-message candidates for explicit facts
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from multiple messages that describe the same event, verify that all explicit factual statements from each source message are included in the candidate before finalizing.
content: When extracting a memory candidate from multiple messages, after drafting the candidate, re-read each source message and confirm that every explicit fact (activities, dates, locations, preferences, outcomes) is represented. If a fact is missing, add it to the candidate before emitting it.

candidates.solves: A memory candidate built from multiple messages about one event omitted an explicit activity from a later source message, causing incomplete memories. The rule is to verify each candidate against all source messages and include every explicit fact. It applies whenever extraction merges multiple messages into one candidate, across any topic such as trips or projects.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Object Descriptions as Candidates
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker describing an item they have, are showing, or own, extract a memory candidate for that object and its stated attributes during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, if a statement identifies an item (e.g., 'It's a map of...', 'I have a...', 'This is my...') and gives its type or attributes, generate a candidate memory capturing the item and those attributes.
Do not require the word 'favorite', 'love', or an explicit preference; an item's identity and description are memory-worthy facts.
Keep the candidate grounded in the exact stated attributes; do not infer additional traits beyond the message.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline omitted an explicit fact because the message phrased it as a description of an item ('It's a map of...') rather than as a stated preference or plan, and no candidate was generated. Future sessions need a rule that during extraction, any utterance identifying an object the speaker possesses, shows, or references should produce a compact memory candidate for that object and its stated attributes, independent of the surface topic.

payload.name: PreserveAllStatedFactsWhenExtractingActivityDetails
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message that describes an activity with multiple distinct facets, or before accepting an UPDATE/MERGE that enriches an event memory, use all stated facts from the source and drop none.
content: During extraction, if a message describes an activity with several distinct facts (e.g., what the subject does, what companions or pets do, outcomes, social benefits), include every stated fact in the candidate content; do not omit a fact because it is tangential to the existing memory's current focus.

Before accepting an UPDATE or MERGE, compare the proposed new memory content against the source message; if any stated fact from the source is absent from both the candidate and the existing memory, add it to the candidate or create a separate candidate so the memory remains complete.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates that describe a recurring activity sometimes keep only the facts aligned with the existing memory's topic and drop other stated details, leaving memories incomplete. This rule applies when a message lists multiple distinct facets of one activity (what the subject does, what companions or pets do, social outcomes) and requires preserving every independent fact in extraction and in later UPDATE/MERGE verification. It does not require adding unstated inferences or merging unrelated topics.

payload.name: Preserve All Explicit Actions During Extraction
payload.description: When a user message lists multiple concrete actions taken in response to an event, use during extraction and updates to ensure every explicit action is captured in memory rather than replaced by a general summary.
content: During candidate extraction, when a message describes a sequence of concrete actions taken by a person, preserve every discrete action in the extracted memory content; do not replace the action list with only an inferred general relationship, feeling, or attribute.

During update or merge, before modifying an existing memory, check the source message for explicitly stated actions; if any action is missing from the current memory content, add those missing concrete details to the updated version rather than only enriching with broader inferences.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that candidate extraction omitted all four concrete calming actions from a message and kept only the inferred bond statement, so later recall of those actions failed. The reusable mechanism is extracting a general relational summary instead of preserving explicitly enumerated actions. This applies to any future conversation where a speaker lists multiple discrete actions in response to an event; memory must retain every stated action to answer 'how' questions.

payload.name: Preserve explicit categories over examples
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from statements that name broad categories followed by examples, use this to keep the explicit high-level wording instead of only concrete examples.
content: During candidate extraction, when a statement names a high-level category, goal, or interest and then gives concrete examples, preserve the explicit high-level wording in the candidate; do not replace it with only the examples.
If a statement includes both a general category and examples, include both when possible; if only one fits, keep the general category because future questions may target it.

After drafting a candidate, compare it with the source message for any explicitly stated abstract terms; if they are missing and only examples remain, revise the candidate to retain the abstract terms.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is extraction summarization that dropped a speaker's explicitly stated category and kept only concrete examples, so the memory could not answer a later question about the category. This occurs whenever a speaker names a broad category or goal and then illustrates it with examples; the extractor keeps examples but drops the category. The rule applies to future construction extraction across topics, not to retrieval-side or memory-kind decisions.

payload.name: Extract per-entity attributes from multi-entity lists
payload.description: When a user message assigns distinct attributes to multiple identified entities (e.g., each pet's personality, each family member's trait), extract one memory candidate per entity during construction.
content: During extraction, if a user message assigns distinct attributes to multiple identified entities (named, ordinal, or otherwise), create one candidate for each entity-attribute pair; do not skip the message or collapse the list into a single aggregate candidate.
Include the entity descriptor (e.g., oldest, second, name) and the specific attribute in the candidate text, and bind it to the source message so each fact is independently retrievable.
Apply this rule to any entity type (pets, people, groups) and use an existing memory kind that fits the stable attribute; do not invent new memory kinds.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes ingests a user message listing separate attributes for multiple entities (e.g., each pet's personality) but produces no extraction candidates, losing all listed facts. This rule directs extraction to split such multi-entity attribute lists into per-entity candidates so each fact is independently recallable. It applies whenever a speaker assigns distinct characteristics to each member of a group, but not when the message describes the group as a whole.

payload.name: Preserve concrete item type for product lines
payload.description: When extracting memories about a limited edition line, collection, or series, if the message explicitly names an example item type, preserve that type instead of only recording the generic 'line'.
content: During extraction, when a speaker introduces a product or creative work by pointing to a concrete example item and then says it belongs to a limited line, collection, or series, record the concrete item type as the object of the memory (e.g., 'made limited-edition hoodies'), not just 'made a limited edition line'.
When the concrete item noun appears earlier in the same message or nearby turns and is clearly the referent of the line/collection, use that noun even if the later sentence only says 'line'.

candidates.solves: Extraction often condenses a described line or collection to a generic label and drops the concrete item type the speaker explicitly attached to it (e.g., 'this hoodie ... limited edition line' loses 'hoodie'). This rule instructs extractors to preserve the specific noun in memory so future questions about what was made can be answered. It applies whenever a message ties a named example item to a broader series, but not when the item type is hypothetical or not explicitly identified.

payload.name: CaptureAllEnumeratedItems
payload.description: When a user message lists multiple distinct items, extract and retain every item in memory content; do not omit any when summarizing or updating.
content: During extraction, if a message enumerates two or more distinct items (e.g., separated by commas, conjunctions, or bullet points), include each item explicitly in the candidate content. Avoid summaries that may drop list elements; paraphrase minimally and keep all listed specifics.

During CRUD, compare new evidence against existing memories: if an item from an enumerated list is missing from the stored memory, update or merge to add that item rather than leaving the memory incomplete.

candidates.solves: Memory construction often loses details when a speaker enumerates multiple distinct items in one message; the resulting memory is incomplete and fails to support claims about dropped elements. This skill ensures extraction and CRUD preserve every explicitly listed item, so future questions about any element can be answered. It applies to any topic where a user lists multiple attributes, reasons, preferences, or experiences.

payload.name: Preserve enumerated specifics in extraction
payload.description: When a message lists multiple distinct actions, behaviors, or reasons connected by 'and' or commas, apply this before creating or updating a candidate memory to avoid collapsing them into one umbrella term.
content: Before writing a candidate from raw evidence, identify every distinct action, behavior, or mechanism the speaker lists (e.g., 'help and push each other').
Preserve each listed specific in the memory content, using close paraphrase; do not replace the whole list with a broader term like 'support' that omits one component.
If updating an existing memory, merge all enumerated specifics from the new evidence into the updated content rather than keeping only the first or most salient one.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a candidate paraphrased 'help and push each other' as 'support each other', dropping the specific 'push' component, so the memory only partially supported the reference claim. The failure mechanism is over-abstraction of conjunctive specifics in raw evidence. This rule applies whenever future messages enumerate multiple distinct actions, benefits, or reasons and the extraction step must retain each component to answer targeted questions.

payload.name: Extract enumerated recommended items
payload.description: When a message explicitly lists items one person recommends, provides, or selects for another, include the concrete items in the extracted memory instead of summarizing them as 'supplies' or 'help.'
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly enumerates specific items they recommend, provide, or choose for someone, record each concrete item in the candidate content; do not replace the list with a generic phrase like 'recommended supplies' or 'offered to help.'
When updating an existing memory, preserve and add the explicit item details from the current message; avoid summarization that drops named objects needed to answer future questions.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often summarizes that someone recommended or offered help while dropping the concrete items named in the message. This causes later questions about the specific recommended items to be unsupported. This skill applies whenever a message enumerates tangible items (supplies, tools, ingredients, equipment, etc.) in a recommendation, offer, plan, or transfer; future sessions asking what was recommended or needed should retrieve an itemized memory.

payload.name: Preserve-specific-recommendations-in-extraction
payload.description: During construction extraction, when a message contains specific advice, substitutions, or named recommendations, ensure the memory stores the concrete details rather than only a generic summary of interest or assistance.
content: When extracting from a message that names specific suggestions, substitutions, or tips, encode those concrete details in the memory content; do not reduce the message to a general statement about interest, help, or participation.
If a candidate only summarizes the speaker's general attitude but omits named items, revise it to include the factual recommendation before marking it ADD or UPDATE.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes summarize a speaker's general interest or offer of help while omitting the concrete substitutions or recommendations in the same message, leaving future questions about those specifics unanswerable. This Skill applies whenever a source message contains named advice, substitutions, or tips: the extracted memory must preserve those concrete facts instead of only the generic intent. It does not apply to messages containing only general statements with no specific recommendation.

payload.name: CaptureAllListedOptionsInMemory
payload.description: When a source message lists multiple options or alternatives (e.g., 'or', 'and', comma-separated), apply during extraction to keep all listed items in memory; do not drop items because later dialogue focuses on one.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source message explicitly enumerates two or more options/items (using 'or', 'and', commas, or slashes), include every enumerated item in the extracted memory content; do not omit one just because later messages elaborate only another.

When preparing an ADD or UPDATE, compare the proposed memory with its source evidence: if the evidence lists multiple distinct items, ensure each appears in the memory (or in another linked memory); if an existing memory omits an item from the same source, update it to add the missing item.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often drop one alternative from a source message when later conversation focuses on another, leaving memory incomplete. This skill enforces completeness for explicitly enumerated options/lists in a single message, across topics. It applies during extraction and CRUD whenever a statement lists multiple items; it does not apply to single-item statements or to inferences beyond the evidence.

payload.name: Maintain-explicit-aggregate-counts-for-recurring-acquisitions
payload.description: When a conversation reveals multiple items in the same countable category for one person across separate messages, create or update an explicit total-count state memory during extraction and CRUD, not only individual event memories.
content: During extraction and CRUD, when a message adds a new item to a countable set already present in memory (e.g., pet, child, vehicle, book), also create or update a `state` memory for the owner that explicitly states the cumulative total (e.g., 'X has N pets').

Before writing the aggregate state, count all distinct items for that owner and category using existing memories plus the current message; do not rely on implication or leave the total for a future question to infer.
If an aggregate state memory already exists, UPDATE it with the new total and timestamp of the latest evidence; if none exists, ADD one. Preserve the individual item memories for traceability.

candidates.solves: Construction logged each added item (pet, child, vehicle, book) as an event but never saved an explicit cumulative count, so 'how many' questions were only partially answered. The failure is omitting an aggregate count when the same countable category grows across messages. Apply to any future multi-message accumulation of countable items for one owner; not to single one-off item mentions.

payload.name: Preserve explicit enumerations during extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from a message that lists multiple distinct aspects, reasons, or outcomes, preserve all listed items in the memory content.
content: During candidate extraction, if source text explicitly lists multiple distinct qualities, reasons, outcomes, or preferences, include every listed item in the memory content. Do not silently drop any item while paraphrasing; if compressing, use a phrase that still covers all enumerated details.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can drop items when paraphrasing an explicit enumeration, causing partial memory coverage. This skill applies when a source message lists multiple distinct qualities, reasons, outcomes, or preferences and a candidate memory is being created; it does not apply to inferred conclusions or to compressing redundant restatements. Preserving all listed items keeps future answers complete.

payload.name: PreserveObjectOfCreationEvents
payload.description: When a message says a person made/created/produced a named thing, include that object in the extracted memory before ADD or UPDATE.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source describes someone making/creating/producing something (including a line, collection, edition, or item), the extracted memory must state the explicit object; do not summarize the action alone.
Before ADD/UPDATE/MERGE, check that any direct object of a creation verb from the source appears in the candidate or target memory; if missing, include it.
Do not invent an object that is not present in the evidence.

candidates.solves: During extraction, the direct object of creation verbs like 'made' or 'created' is sometimes dropped, leaving a memory that records the action but not what was produced. This makes future questions like 'made what?' unanswerable. The rule requires preserving any explicitly named object of a creation/production event. It applies to messages describing someone making, designing, or producing a concrete thing, and does not apply when the source itself does not name an object.

payload.name: Store Explicit Counts for Enumerated Sets
payload.description: When constructing memories from a message that introduces or names a new member of a countable set (e.g., pets, children, vehicles) and the full set is explicitly enumerated in the conversation, include the explicit total count in the extracted candidate or memory update.
content: During extraction, when a message names a new member of a countable set (pets, children, vehicles, etc.) and the conversation explicitly enumerates all current members, include the explicit total count in the candidate content, not just the individual member.

During CRUD, when ADDing or UPDATEing a memory that describes a set of named items, ensure the stored content contains the explicit aggregate count if the source conversation supports it; do not rely on the reader to count separate memories.

candidates.solves: Future questions asking 'how many' of a person's countable possessions (pets, children, vehicles) fail when memory contains individual named entries but no explicit total. The diagnosed cause is extraction recording each new member without synthesizing the aggregate count, even when the conversation enumerates the complete set. The reusable rule is to store the explicit total whenever all members are named in the source; it does not apply when the set is only partially mentioned or the count must be guessed.

payload.name: Preserve explicit adjectives in memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a statement in which the speaker explicitly describes a subject with a specific adjective, keep that exact descriptor in the candidate memory content.
content: During extraction or update, if the source directly describes a subject with an explicit adjective or qualifier, include that exact adjective in the memory content. Do not replace precise evaluative words with broader paraphrases or implications. Only include descriptors that are explicitly supported by the source; do not infer unstated ones.

candidates.solves: When a source explicitly applies an adjective to a subject, extraction can drop that specific descriptor while keeping a broader implication, so later factual questions miss the exact claim. Preserve explicitly stated evaluative adjectives in the memory content rather than replacing them with paraphrase. This applies to any future extraction where a speaker directly characterizes something; it does not require inferring descriptors not stated.

payload.name: Extract exact object of missing or longing
payload.description: When a speaker says they miss, long for, or are nostalgic about something and then states the specific aspect in an exclamation or follow-up phrase, before creating or updating a memory ensure that exact aspect is included.
content: During extraction, if a speaker expresses missing or longing for an activity, identify the exact noun phrase they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments') and record it as the object, not just the broader activity summary. Include any clarifying exclamation that follows. When updating or merging, preserve this specific object rather than replacing it with a generic paraphrase.
