candidates.solves: When a speaker says they miss an activity but does not name any specific aspect, a concise activity summary is sufficient. The failure occurs when the speaker follows with an exclamation naming a precise thing they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments'), and the extraction keeps only the broad activity, losing the exact object. This skill adds the rule to capture the specific noun phrase from the exclamation as the object of missing. Future sessions with 'miss', 'long for', or 'nostalgic' statements that clarify a particular aspect will benefit. It does not apply when no specific aspect is named.

payload.name: Separate speaker-specific feelings during extraction
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when multiple speakers share personal feelings or reactions in a conversation; create separate memories per speaker instead of merging them.
content: During extraction, when one speaker states their own feeling or inspiration and another speaker then shares a different feeling or reaction, create a separate candidate memory for each speaker's self-attributed statement.
Do not merge the second speaker's response into the first speaker's memory; preserve the exact speaker as the subject of each 'I feel' or 'I think' statement.
If a memory candidate aggregates multiple turns, verify that every distinct speaker's claim is represented in its own candidate before deciding to add.

candidates.solves: A construction extraction failure occurred when one speaker's feeling was captured but another speaker's contrasting feeling in the same exchange was dropped, leaving later questions about the second speaker unanswerable. The reusable rule is to extract each participant's self-attributed feeling as its own memory during multi-turn conversations, preserving speaker boundaries. This applies to any multi-party dialogue where feelings, preferences, or opinions are exchanged.

payload.name: Preserve Direct Answers in Extraction
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about how they learned or acquired a skill, include that answer as a distinct fact during extraction and keep it when updating an existing memory.
content: During extraction, list every discrete factual statement in a message; do not omit facts merely because they do not match the main theme of an existing memory.

When a message directly answers a question about how, when, or from whom the speaker learned a skill, always capture that answer (e.g., self-taught, taught by someone, learned at a certain age) as part of the candidate content.

When updating an existing memory, preserve all newly stated details in the enriched content or create an additional candidate; do not select just the facts that expand the current memory and drop the direct answer.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often keep only facts that align with an existing memory theme and silently drop other directly stated facts, such as how someone learned a skill (self-taught vs taught). This matters when a later question asks about that dropped fact. The Skill instructs extraction to capture every discrete fact from a message, especially direct answers to questions about acquisition or ability, and to preserve those facts when enriching an existing memory.

payload.name: Extract nickname relationships from address terms
payload.description: When a dialogue message contains a speaker addressing another person by a name that differs from the addressee's full name, extract a nickname relationship even if the message's main topic is an event.
content: During extraction, scan direct-address terms (greetings, vocatives) in each message and compare them against the full names of the conversation participants.
When a direct-address term is a shortened or alternative form of a participant's full name, create a relationship memory recording that the speaker uses that term as a nickname for that participant.
Add this nickname relationship independently of any event/state memory extracted from the same message; do not drop address terms because another fact seems more salient.

candidates.solves: The construction extraction step can over-focus on a message's main event and discard direct-address nicknames as incidental, leaving later nickname queries unanswerable. The reusable fix is to treat any non-full-name address term as an independent relationship fact during extraction. This applies to future dialogue where a nickname appears in a greeting or vocative; it does not apply to generic pronouns, formal titles, or address terms matching the full name.

payload.name: Preserve all distinct claims in multi-claim utterances
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from an utterance that describes multiple distinct activities, hobbies, or topics each with its own value, feeling, or outcome, ensure each distinct claim is preserved.
content: During candidate extraction, treat an utterance containing multiple independent claims as a set of distinct memory candidates; do not let one salient claim suppress another.
If combining claims into one memory, include every subject and its specific predicate; if any claim cannot be combined cleanly, emit a separate ADD candidate so all evidence-backed facts survive.

candidates.solves: A speaker utterance describes multiple distinct activities or topics, each with its own evaluation or benefit, and extraction preserves only the most salient claim, losing other evidence-backed facts. This skill applies whenever constructing memories from multi-claim utterances in any future session, regardless of topic, and does not require knowing the gold answer.

payload.name: CaptureDirectDisclosureRecipient
payload.description: When a user directly tells a conversation partner about a personal life event, extract the act of telling that partner as a durable fact, not just the event itself.
content: During extraction, if a message is a direct address (e.g., 'Hey Sam, ...') and the speaker discloses a personal event (marriage, job, move, health, etc.), create a memory that records both the event and that the speaker informed that specific addressee.
Do not drop the addressee as conversational framing; later questions may ask who was told.
Do not apply this to generic statements, third-party news, or non-durable small talk.

candidates.solves: The failure was an extraction candidate that captured a marriage announcement but omitted that the speaker told Sam, so later memory could not answer 'who did X tell?'. This skill applies whenever a directly addressed disclosure of a personal event occurs, and requires recording the recipient of the disclosure. It does not apply to third-party statements or non-durable routine small talk.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-evaluative experience statements
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about their own recent experience with an overall assessment and specific positive/negative details, use during candidate extraction to capture the explicit statement as a memory candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly describes the speaker's own recent experience, outcome, or season with an overall assessment and supporting positive/negative details, create a memory candidate for that description; do not skip it merely because it is conversational or mixed in sentiment.
Preserve the key facts and the overall assessment in the candidate, and include any concrete outcome (e.g., a win or loss) as part of the same or a linked event candidate when available.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because an explicit first-person evaluative statement answering a question about the speaker's own team season was not extracted as a candidate, so no memory was persisted. The abstract mechanism is missing extraction of direct self-reports that combine an overall assessment with specific positives/negatives. This rule applies to future sessions where a user or assistant characterizes their own experience, project, or outcome in response to a question; it does not cover inferring unstated opinions or summarizing third-party facts.

payload.name: Extract reported third-party condition assessments
payload.description: When a message contains a third-party reported assessment (e.g., doctor's statement) about a person's condition, use during extraction to create a state memory for the assessed person.
content: During extraction, if a speaker reports what a third party (doctor, specialist, etc.) said about someone's condition, create a `state` candidate about the person whose condition is assessed. Include the assessment and date/session time when known.
Keep this as a separate candidate even when the same message also expresses support or describes the speaker's own situation.
Resolve the assessed subject from the conversation context, not from the current speaker, and apply this to any reported evaluation.

candidates.solves: During construction, a speaker often relays a third party's assessment of someone's condition (e.g., 'doctor said not serious') inside a supportive reply, and extraction can miss it by focusing on the speaker's own state or on mutual support. Use this to extract reported evaluations as durable state facts about the person discussed. Applies to any reported authoritative evaluation; not retrieval-side answer selection.

payload.name: Preserve Direct Speaker Statements in Memories
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker's direct statement or quotation to another person, ensure extracted or updated memory content includes the speaker's words and attribution, not just the listener's reaction.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a direct quote or specific statement from a speaker about an event, plan, or relationship, preserve the speaker's words (or close paraphrase) and the speaker's identity in the memory candidate, rather than summarizing only the listener's reaction or the event from the listener's perspective.
When updating existing memories, if a new message includes a speaker's direct statement that adds a fact or quote not yet stored, incorporate that statement with its speaker attribution.

candidates.solves: Construction candidates often summarize an exchange from the listener's perspective, omitting the speaker's direct words (e.g., a quote) and attributing the sentiment to the wrong person. This rule abstracts the failure to require preserving speaker identity and quoted content when a message contains a clear statement, and applies to future sessions where a specific person says something memorable or plan-relevant.

payload.name: Preserve co-participants in extracted events
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message reports an event shared by the speaker and another person using inclusive phrases (e.g., 'we', 'my partner and I', 'my friend and I'); extract the memory with all participants included.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source message describes an event or activity involving multiple people through inclusive phrases such as 'we', 'my partner and I', or 'my friend and I', include every named or clearly implied participant in the extracted content.
Do not reduce a plural subject to only the speaker; preserve the joint nature of the event even if the other participant is not named again in later messages.
When another participant is not explicitly named, record their role or relationship (e.g., 'with partner', 'with friend') instead of omitting them from the event memory.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction omitted the speaker's travel companion from a joint event memory, so later queries about the companion were unsupported. The abstract mechanism is that extraction summaries often collapse first-person plural statements ('my partner and I', 'we') into the speaker alone. This rule applies to future construction extraction whenever a message reports an activity shared with others, instructing the system to preserve all named or clearly implied participants. It does not apply to CRUD operations or solo-activity memories.

payload.name: Extract third-party progress praise statements
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker makes an explicit evaluative statement about another person's progress, achievement, or effort, create a memory candidate preserving the speaker's claim.
content: During extraction, treat a speaker's evaluative statement about a specific other person's progress, achievement, or effort as a candidate fact attributable to the speaker, even when phrased as praise or encouragement (e.g., 'your hard work is paying off').
Record the target person and the claimed state/outcome as a compact state or relationship memory, linked to the speaker's utterance as evidence.
Do not skip such statements because they are complimentary or because the target is not the speaker.

candidates.solves: Messages where one person explicitly assesses another's progress are often skipped as mere praise, so later queries about 'what did X say about Y's progress?' fail. This skill makes extraction preserve such speaker-attributed evaluative statements. Applies to any named third party and progress comments; not to generic aphorisms without a specific subject or internal plans.

payload.name: Extract-multiple-independent-facts-per-message
payload.description: When a message or conversational turn contains independent durable facts about more than one person or topic, use this during extraction to create a separate candidate for each fact instead of keeping only one.
content: During candidate extraction, scan the full message for every clause that states a distinct durable fact (event, achievement, preference, state) about any person; create one candidate per fact, even when a reply mentions another person's activity.

When two speakers' facts appear in one exchange (e.g., one person reports an achievement and the other mentions their own trip), do not choose one subject; emit separate event/state memories for each.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction failures in construction when a single message or exchange contains independent durable facts about more than one person. The diagnosed cause was that extraction recorded only Joanna's road trip and omitted Nate's explicitly stated video game tournament win. The rule to enumerate each distinct fact as a separate candidate generalizes to any future multi-fact message, and it does not apply to CRUD operations or to merging related details.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Social Interaction Events
payload.description: When a message explicitly states a social interaction (e.g., skyped, met, talked, visited) with a person and what was discussed or shared, create an extraction candidate for the interaction and topic.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly mentions that someone interacted with another person (by skype, meeting, talk, visit, etc.) and states the topic or shared content, create an event or relationship candidate with the participants, action, topic, and any stated time.
Do not skip such a candidate simply because the interaction is mentioned in casual conversation; record it when it is specific enough to answer a future question about the interaction.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a message explicitly reporting a social interaction (skyped with a fan, discussed characters) produced no extraction candidate, so the fact was never stored. The abstract failure is that explicit interaction statements with a topic can be overlooked during candidate extraction. This rule applies to any future message that states an interaction between people and its topic, and where that fact might later be queried.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitMediaFactsDuringExtraction
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message states a concrete fact about a shared photo, video, or other media (e.g., location, date, subject) while also containing general commentary; preserve the factual detail explicitly.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a concrete fact about shared media (e.g., where or when a photo was taken, who is in it), create a candidate that states that fact directly; do not let a broader discussion/theme candidate replace it.
When a message mixes factual detail with reflective commentary, store the factual claim separately from any general theme; both may be valid memories, but the fact must not be omitted.
Before accepting an ADD candidate, check that every directly stated factual detail that could answer a future question is retained; a candidate that only restates the topic is incomplete.

candidates.solves: Concrete factual details about shared media (e.g., a photo's location) are often lost when extraction creates only a general discussion memory. This rule requires preserving such explicit facts as standalone candidates whenever a message mixes a factual statement with commentary. Applies to any media-related fact (location, time, subject); not to purely opinion/theme summaries.

payload.name: Infer writing from online forum discussion
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a user mentions joining or participating in an online forum/community and describes talking, discussing, or chatting about topics; record that they write comments/posts on those topics.
content: If a user says they joined or participate in an online forum/community and mentions talking, discussing, or chatting about subjects, extract an event memory stating they write comments/posts on those subjects, not just that they participated or talked.
Do not apply if the user explicitly indicates reading only, lurking, or offline conversations.
Preserve the subject and topics from the message exactly; use memory kind 'event', and set subject to the user.

candidates.solves: The extraction step omitted the writing aspect of a user's participation in an online forum, recording only that they joined and discussed topics. This skill ensures that when a user mentions discussing/talking in an online forum or community, the memory includes that they write comments/posts on those topics, because online forum discussions are written communications. It applies to any future message where forum/community participation is described with discussion verbs.

payload.name: Extract subject facts from partner confirmations
payload.description: When a conversational partner refers to something the subject shared or did and names or describes it, extract a memory for the subject from that confirming detail.
content: During extraction, consider messages from all participants as potential evidence about the subject, not only the subject's own statements.

If a reply names, labels, or describes something the subject shared or did in a prior message, generate a candidate event memory for the subject that includes that concrete detail, grounded in both the original message and the confirming reply.
Do not let the absence of the subject's own explicit label prevent extraction when a partner's direct attribution supplies it.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often ignores factual claims made by a conversational partner about the subject, especially when the partner comments on media or an activity the subject shared (e.g., labeling a posted meal). This causes missing memories. The proposed rule directs extraction to treat direct third-party attributions as candidate evidence for subject events, so future sessions capture facts that are only stated by the other speaker.

payload.name: Preserve Companion in Shared Activity Extraction
payload.description: When constructing memories from conversation and a user describes an activity or preference with 'we', 'us', or 'together', retrieve this Skill to ensure the companion and shared activity are captured.
content: During extraction, when a message uses first-person plural ('we', 'us', 'our') or 'together' to express an activity or preference, create a candidate that names the companion (if identifiable from conversation) and the shared activity.
Do not merge the shared activity only into a memory about the speaker alone; preserve it as a joint activity with the companion, using 'event' or 'relationship' memory kind as appropriate.
If the companion is not explicit, use the most recent person the speaker was discussing or leave the companion as the implied co-participant rather than dropping it.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the activity when a speaker uses first-person plural, losing the companion and the relational fact. This Skill addresses that by requiring the companion and shared activity to be extracted together, enabling future questions about joint activities. It applies to any conversation where activities or preferences are expressed with 'we' or 'together'.

payload.name: Extract distinct factual claims from multi-turn dialogue
payload.description: When constructing memories from a multi-turn conversation, if a speaker states a specific effect or personal fact (e.g., how an activity makes them feel), extract it as its own memory instead of merging it into a broad conversation summary.
content: During extraction, parse each speaker turn for explicit self-referential claims (activities, feelings, preferences, routines). Create a separate memory for each such claim, using the speaker as subject and the appropriate memory kind (e.g., preference or state).

Do not reduce a multi-topic conversation to a single event memory that only lists discussed topics; ensure every explicit factual statement with lasting relevance is represented in its own memory entry.
If a claim is made in response to a question, still treat it as a durable stated belief and record it independently.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure is that the construction agent collapsed a multi-turn conversation into one event summary, omitting an explicit statement that exercise makes the speaker feel connected to her body. The reusable problem is extraction over-summarization: any time a conversation contains multiple distinct self-disclosures, a single event memory cannot preserve them. This rule applies to future multi-turn dialogues where speakers state specific effects, preferences, or routines, and directs the agent to emit one memory per durable claim.

payload.name: Preserve directly-stated facts during extraction
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a factual question (e.g., how they met, when, where), extract that specific fact as its own memory candidate during extraction instead of only creating a high-level conversation summary.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a direct answer to a factual question (how, when, where, how long), create a separate candidate that captures the specific fact exactly, in addition to any broader conversation summary.
Do not replace an explicit fact with a generic paraphrase (e.g., 'shared experiences about her relationship'); preserve the concrete detail so it remains retrievable later.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction summarized the conversation and lost an explicitly stated fact (how a couple met). The mechanism is over-generalization during candidate extraction, which can drop any directly stated fact. This applies to any session where a speaker directly answers a factual question and that fact must remain retrievable; it does not apply to indirect statements.

payload.name: Preserve_All_Enumerated_Components_In_Extraction
payload.description: When a single message gives advice, strategies, preferences, or facts as multiple distinct items joined by 'and', 'or', commas, or bullets, during extraction preserve every component in the memory content; do not drop any listed element.
content: During extraction, when a single message contains multiple distinct components of advice, strategies, preferences, or facts linked by 'and', 'or', commas, or bullets, preserve every component in the candidate content. Do not collapse the list to one item; check each connector clause and include it explicitly.
Apply the same completeness check when writing or updating memories from such messages: confirm that each enumerated item in the source maps to a distinct phrase in the memory content.

candidates.solves: Extraction dropped the 'set goals' component from a multi-part study tip. The mechanism is incomplete extraction of enumerated components from a single utterance. This rule preserves all explicitly listed components during extraction, transferring to any future construction where advice or preferences are delivered as a list, but not to intentional merges or single-fact messages.

payload.name: Preserve explicit facts during candidate extraction and CRUD
payload.description: When a user message states multiple distinct facts, especially activities plus objects, accessories, or answers to direct questions, use separate extraction candidates and verify none are dropped before UPDATE or MERGE.
content: During extraction, when a single user message states multiple distinct explicit facts, do not consolidate them into one activity-focused summary. Create separate candidates for facts about objects, accessories, clothing, preferences, or answers to direct questions, ensuring every explicit claim appears in at least one candidate.

Before applying an UPDATE, MERGE, or ADD, re-check the candidate against its source messages; if an explicit fact is missing, add it to the candidate or create an additional candidate rather than letting it be dropped.
When a fact does not fit an existing memory's dominant theme, record it as its own ADD candidate instead of omitting it or forcing it into an unrelated enrichment.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction collapsed a multi-fact message into one activity summary, omitting an explicit object/accessory fact that later questions rely on. The reusable failure is incomplete candidate coverage when a message mixes activities with separate objects, preferences, or answers to direct questions. The rule requires every explicit claim to survive in some candidate, using separate ADD candidates when facts do not share the dominant theme. It applies to any future extraction/CRUD session with multi-fact user messages; it does not apply to inferring facts the user never stated.

payload.name: PreserveAllActivityComponents
payload.description: When extracting an activity that covers multiple distinct areas or topics, ensure every area is kept as an equal component in the memory content.
content: During extraction, when a memory subject performs an activity (seminar, class, program, campaign, etc.) covering multiple distinct areas or topics, represent each area as an equal component in the memory content (e.g., 'seminars on X and Y'), not as a modifier of the first area.

Before creating an ADD/UPDATE candidate, scan the source for all explicitly listed areas linked by 'and', 'as well as', or 'plus'; confirm each appears in the candidate's content and object fields; if any is missing, revise the candidate.

candidates.solves: When a source describes one activity spanning multiple distinct areas (e.g., seminars on sports and marketing), extraction may treat the first area as the activity type and demote others, losing a fact. This skill requires storing all listed areas as equal components. It applies to any activity with a conjunctive list in future sessions, and does not apply when only one area is truly named.

payload.name: ExtractAdditionalHobbiesAfterAlso
payload.description: When a user describes a person's hobbies or interests and later adds another with 'also', 'too', or 'and', extract the additional one as a separate durable fact.
content: During extraction, if a user states a hobby/interest for a person and then in a later turn adds another hobby/interest with 'also', 'too', or 'and', create a separate candidate memory for the additional item.
Do not treat the later item as a paraphrase of the earlier statement or skip it because the topic was already captured; each explicitly named hobby or interest is a distinct fact.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes drops a second hobby or interest when the user adds it in a follow-up turn with 'also' after a previous turn already yielded a memory. The rule forces extraction of each explicitly named attribute separately, preventing incomplete memory profiles. Applies to any conversation where a person's hobbies or interests are enumerated across adjacent turns.

payload.name: Preserve-all-enumerated-hobbies-and-interests
payload.description: When a user explicitly names multiple hobbies, interests, or enjoyed activities in one message, apply during extraction and CRUD to ensure every listed item is stored, not just the first or most elaborated one.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly enumerates a person's hobbies, interests, or enjoyed activities (e.g., 'X and Y' or 'A, B, and C'), preserve every listed item in memory candidates. Do not drop secondary items because they receive less explanation or emphasis.
If the message elaborates on only one item, still capture the other listed items in the same or separate candidates so the complete preference set is stored.

During CRUD, before accepting an ADD, compare the candidate against the source message; if any explicitly listed hobby/interest item is missing, supplement the candidate or update the existing memory instead of committing an incomplete one.

candidates.solves: When extracting memories from a message where a user explicitly lists several hobbies, interests, or enjoyed activities, the constructor may capture only the first or elaborated item and omit the rest, leaving the memory incomplete for later questions. This Skill enforces that all enumerated items in such statements are preserved, avoiding missing preference claims. It applies to any future message with explicit multi-item hobby/interest/enjoyment lists, not to implied or vague statements.

payload.name: Extract-All-Enumerated-Items
payload.description: When a user message contains multiple listed pieces of advice, preferences, facts, or requirements, use during extraction to capture every item instead of only the first few.
content: When extracting candidates from a message that presents several distinct items in a list (numbered, bulleted, or natural-language 'also/and'), include all enumerated items. Combine them into one candidate if they share a subject, or create separate candidates; do not drop trailing items. Before finalizing an extraction candidate, recheck the raw message to confirm every listed item is represented.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction candidate omitted the last piece of advice from an enumerated list, so later ADD only persisted partial information. The abstraction: any extraction step must treat enumerations as complete sets and preserve every listed item. This applies whenever future messages contain multiple distinct advice, preferences, or facts in one utterance; it does not require knowing the gold answer and is not limited to a particular topic.

payload.name: Preserve all explicit feelings in extraction
payload.description: When a message explicitly states multiple feelings or attributes about the same activity or subject, include all of them in the extracted memory candidate instead of selecting only one.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source text explicitly lists multiple distinct feelings, preferences, or attributes about the same subject or activity (e.g., 'exciting and free-feeling'), capture every listed element in the memory content. Do not drop any explicit descriptor even if one seems more salient; paraphrase only to combine them concisely.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often drop one of multiple explicitly stated feelings about the same activity, losing a claim. The rule: when a message lists multiple distinct feelings or attributes, retain all explicit descriptors. This applies to any future extraction where a single subject has several explicit evaluative terms.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly listed elements in extracted memories
payload.description: When a message explicitly lists two or more distinct topics, activities, preferences, or facts (e.g., joined by 'and' or commas), extract each element separately instead of merging or dropping any.
content: During extraction: if the source statement explicitly enumerates multiple items, topics, activities, preferences, or facts (e.g., 'dreams and life'), include every listed element in the candidate memory content. Do not replace the full list with a single umbrella phrase or omit any item.
When updating existing memories, preserve all previously recorded listed elements unless the new message explicitly changes or removes one.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: candidate extraction paraphrased an explicitly enumerated pair ('dreams and life') into a single theme, dropping one element. The reusable failure mechanism is lossy summarization of explicit lists during memory extraction. This applies to future conversations where a speaker enumerates multiple topics, activities, preferences, or facts in one clause; the extracted memory should retain every listed element so later questions can be answered completely.

payload.name: Preserve all components of stated symbolic meanings
payload.description: When a speaker explains what something symbolizes, stands for, or means and lists multiple aspects, preserve every listed component during extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source text describes what something symbolizes, stands for, or represents and mentions multiple components, keep every explicitly stated component in the candidate content.
Do not replace a specific listed component (activity, context, or purpose) with a broader paraphrase that drops it; include the full set of meanings exactly as stated.

candidates.solves: During construction extraction, candidates may paraphrase a multi-part symbolic meaning and drop one explicitly stated component, leaving memory incomplete and future answers wrong. This skill is a reusable extraction rule: when source text defines what something symbolizes, stands for, or means, preserve all listed components rather than summarizing them away. It applies to any future statement that explains the meaning or representation of an object, phrase, tattoo, logo, or action.

payload.name: Preserve-explicit-general-claims-in-event-memories
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from multiple messages, if the speaker explicitly mentions a general activity or category, include that claim as a distinct fact even when specific examples are also recorded.
content: During extraction, when a speaker describes an experience across multiple turns, include every explicitly stated general activity or category in the memory content, even when you also list specific examples—the general claim is independently queryable.
Re-check all source messages for umbrella terms and quantifiers (e.g., 'many', 'various', 'lots of') and represent them in the candidate; do not collapse the umbrella into its examples.

candidates.solves: The extraction candidate summarized a trip by specific activities but omitted the explicit umbrella claim 'went on many excursions', leaving the memory incomplete for a later query about that general activity. The underlying mechanism is dropping a general, independently queryable claim once its examples are captured. This rule applies to any multi-turn event extraction where a speaker states both a category and instances; preserving the category prevents partial-coverage failures.

payload.name: Extract explicit personal resolve statements
payload.description: When a speaker makes an explicit first-person commitment or refusal about their own future behavior (e.g., 'I won't quit'), extract and store it as a memory.
content: Recognize explicit first-person statements of commitment or refusal about the speaker's own future behavior (e.g., 'I won't quit', 'I'm not giving up') as memory-worthy candidates.
Store such statements as a `state` or `plan` memory tied to the speaker, specifying the action/behavior; do not dismiss them as conversational filler or reassurance.

candidates.solves: The construction stage often misses explicit first-person commitments like 'I won't quit' or 'I'm not giving up' because they are phrased negatively or as reassurance. This Skill ensures such statements are extracted and stored as a state/plan memory. It applies to any message where a speaker directly states their own future resolve or refusal; not to hypotheticals, third-party statements, or general advice.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Role and Trait Attributions
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a message where a speaker explicitly states another person's role or qualities, capture the specific attribution instead of reducing it to generic encouragement.
content: During extraction, if a source message contains an explicit statement about a person's role, title, or qualities (e.g., 'you are a perfect mentor', 'your positivity and determination will make it a hit'), create or update a memory candidate that records that specific claim, including the exact trait words used, and do not replace it with a vague paraphrase such as 'encourages' or 'believes in potential'.

When the same message also contains separate encouragement or support, keep the explicit attribution as its own memory candidate or as an explicit, retained part of the candidate content so the fact remains directly answerable later.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an extraction candidate paraphrased an explicit role and trait attribution (being a perfect mentor, having positivity and determination) into generic encouragement, making the fact unanswerable later. This rule addresses any future message where a speaker explicitly attributes a role, title, or personal quality to someone; the reusable failure mechanism is replacing specific claims with vague supportive summaries. It applies during candidate extraction in Construction and prevents the loss of answerable facts before CRUD decisions.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Current Focus Statements in Extraction
payload.description: When a message explicitly states what someone is currently focusing on, doing lately, or prioritizing, preserve that direct claim as a candidate during extraction and do not let supporting examples replace it during CRUD.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement of current focus, priority, or engagement (e.g., 'I've been focusing on X and Y'), create a candidate that records that direct claim even when you also extract concrete examples or activities.
When updating or merging an existing memory with new examples, include both the explicit focus/state claim and the supporting details; do not let the examples substitute for the direct statement.
If the existing memory covers related activities but lacks the explicitly stated current focus, add the focus statement through UPDATE or MERGE rather than only appending the activities.

candidates.solves: Construction candidates often keep the concrete examples from a message but drop the speaker's explicit statement of current focus or priorities. This failure occurred when 'focusing on studying and my relationship' was reduced to only the beach-trip example, so the stored memory lacked the directly stated focus. Future messages that explicitly name what someone is focusing on, doing lately, or prioritizing need the direct state claim preserved alongside any supporting activities.

payload.name: Extract_commitments_as_plan_memories
payload.description: When a speaker promises, offers, or agrees to perform a future action for another person, extract a plan memory even if the action has not yet happened.
content: During extraction, if a speaker promises, offers, or agrees to carry out a future action for another person (e.g., send, write, mail, bring, call, help), extract a candidate plan memory capturing the action, recipient, and topic/object, regardless of whether the action has occurred yet.
During CRUD, when such a commitment appears in the session or retrieved memories, create or update a plan memory; do not dismiss polite offers or future-tense statements as non-memorable.

candidates.solves: Construction pipelines often drop explicit commitments or offers to perform future actions, treating them as non-factual or merely polite statements. This leaves later questions about how something will be done unanswered. The rule applies to any speaker promise/offer/agreement to do a future action for someone else, across topics, and is bounded to action commitments rather than opinions or already-completed events.

payload.name: Capture explicit offers of help or tips
payload.description: During extraction, when a participant explicitly offers assistance, tips, support, or future help to another participant, create a memory recording the offer and its topic.
content: If a message contains an explicit offer by one participant to provide help, tips, support, or future assistance to another, extract a memory capturing that offer.
Record the offering participant, recipient, topic, and the nature of the offer (e.g., support or tips) as an event or relationship memory.
Do not require a completed past action; a stated willingness or availability is sufficient.
Ensure the offer is supported by the message wording and avoid adding details not present.

candidates.solves: Construction pipelines often skip explicit offers of assistance, tips, or future help because the utterance is phrased as a conditional offer rather than a factual statement or preference. This causes missing memories about support commitments. The rule applies whenever extraction processes dialogue where one participant explicitly offers help, tips, or support on a topic to another participant.

payload.name: Extract plans and advice as memory candidates
payload.description: When a conversation contains explicit future intentions, planned actions, or advice/recommendations about what someone should do, extract them as memory candidates before CRUD.
content: During candidate extraction, identify utterances where a speaker states an intention to do something in the future or where one speaker recommends a course of action to another; create a candidate for each such plan or suggestion.

For a stated intention, create a plan candidate capturing the actor and the intended action; for advice or a recommendation, create a relationship or plan candidate capturing the advisor, the advised person, and the recommended action.
Do not drop these candidates merely because the action is described as a future possibility or because the speaker uses tentative language such as 'I will', 'probably', or 'should'.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can skip memory candidates when speakers state future intentions or give advice about those intentions, leaving no durable trace of plans or suggestions. This rule ensures extraction captures such statements as plan/state/relationship candidates whenever a speaker commits to a future action or another speaker recommends one.

payload.name: Extract-explicit-advice-memories
payload.description: When a speaker in the conversation explicitly gives advice, guidance, or a recommendation to another speaker, use this skill during extraction to create a candidate memory for the advice and its recipient/topic.
content: During candidate extraction, identify turns where one participant explicitly advises, recommends, or guides another participant.
Create a candidate memory capturing the advice content, the speaker, the recipient, and the subject/topic, even if the advice is embedded in conversational dialogue.

candidates.solves: The construction agent occasionally omits explicit advice given in conversation, causing facts to be missing from memory. This skill targets the extraction stage to recognize advice-giving turns and generate a candidate memory, preventing such omissions. It applies to any future dialogue where one person gives advice to another.

payload.name: ExtractDirectActionSuggestions
payload.description: When one speaker directly suggests a concrete action for another person, create a memory candidate during extraction; do not skip brief or casual advice.
content: During extraction, generate a candidate whenever a speaker directly tells another person to perform a concrete action, even if the message is short or informal; record the suggested action, the target person, and the speaker.
During CRUD, ADD the suggestion as a compact event or plan memory linked to the source message and timestamp; do not invent details beyond the visible text.

candidates.solves: Construction pipelines sometimes skip direct suggestions when the message is brief or phrased as casual advice. The diagnosed failure was that no candidate was generated for a speaker recommending a concrete action to another person. This rule abstracts that mechanism because suggestions recur across topics and should be stored regardless of surface content. It applies to future sessions where one interlocutor directly advises another to take a concrete action, ensuring the fact is available for later questions. It does not apply to unstated intentions or general praise.

payload.name: Preserve explicit assurance phrases when summarizing endorsements
payload.description: When extracting a memory about someone recommending or promoting a place/experience, include direct positive assurance phrases such as 'you won't regret it' or 'you'll love it' instead of paraphrasing only descriptive details.
content: During extraction, when a speaker is recommending or enticing someone about a place, activity, or experience, capture explicit assurance/evaluative phrases (e.g., 'you won't regret it', 'it's a must-visit', 'you'll never forget it') in the memory candidate, not only descriptive attributes.
When the source message contains both descriptive praise and a direct promise/guarantee about the listener's future satisfaction, preserve both; do not summarize away the emphatic reassurance.

During CRUD, when an existing memory summarizes a recommendation but lacks an explicit assurance phrase present in the source message, issue an UPDATE/MERGE to add that missing claim rather than treating the memory as complete.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was extraction omitting an explicit 'you won't regret it' assurance from a recommendation, leaving the stored memory missing a key claim. This skill addresses the general mechanism of under-capturing emphatic evaluative statements in recommendation summaries. It applies whenever a future session summarizes what someone said while promoting a place, product, or experience.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice as memories
payload.description: When a speaker gives explicit advice, recommendations, or instructions to another person about how to do something, during extraction, create a memory capturing the advice and its topic.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly advises, recommends, or instructs another person on how to do or decide something, create a memory that captures the advice (what was recommended) and the target activity or decision. Use a memory type that fits the fact (e.g., relationship, preference, or event). Do not skip such statements merely because they are short or embedded in a longer exchange.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that the construction agent processed a message containing explicit advice but failed to extract any candidate, so the advice was never persisted. The reusable rule is to treat explicit advice or recommendations from one speaker to another as extraction candidates regardless of the surrounding topic. This applies to any future conversation where a user offers guidance on how to do something and a downstream question may ask about that advice.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Belief-Advice Statements During Ingestion
payload.description: When a participant explicitly tells another what to believe or how to value themselves, extract it as a memory candidate even in supportive/emotional dialogue.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states a belief, value, or guidance they want another participant to adopt (e.g., 'Your worth is not defined by your weight'), create a memory candidate capturing that claim.
Do not ignore such statements because they appear only in encouragement, reassurance, or advice; treat them as durable facts about the speaker's message to the recipient.

When the claim is a directive about self-worth, priorities, or principles, prefer storing it as a preference of the speaker or a state/relationship memory for the recipient, following the session context.

candidates.solves: When a participant explicitly tells another what to believe or how to think about themselves, extraction often overlooks it because the statement is phrased as supportive advice rather than a factual event. This skill ensures such belief-advice statements become memory candidates so future questions about the guidance can be answered from the persisted session. It applies during ingestion of any dialogue where one participant prescribes a value or self-perception to another, but not to mere factual updates or off-topic small talk.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitAttributedValuesSeparately
payload.description: When a message explicitly attributes a value, lesson, or advice to a specific person and the speaker indicates a future intention to follow it, extract that as its own focused memory instead of folding it into a broad conversation summary.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that a specific person stressed or taught a value and the speaker says they want to keep it in mind, create a separate memory capturing that specific value and the person who stressed it, rather than only creating a broad event summary of the conversation.

Before merging into an existing general memory, check that this explicit value/attribution is preserved as its own claim; if the existing memory lacks it, add or update a dedicated memory with the specific value and the person who stressed it.

candidates.solves: Construction fails when a message contains an explicit attribution of a value/lesson to a specific person plus the speaker's stated intent to apply it, because one broad conversation summary omits that durable claim. This rule applies during extraction/CRUD whenever such explicit attributed values occur; it does not apply to general conversation summaries with no explicit attribution.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitFutureGoalsAndAspirations
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement about what the speaker wants to do or achieve in the future, extract it as a memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat explicit future intentions, goals, or aspirations stated by the speaker as extractable memories, even when they describe long-term or post-career plans; do not skip such messages merely because they are reflective.
Represent each stated aspiration as a plan or state candidate tied to the speaker, recording the desired outcome and any optional actions, and link it to the source message.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that a clear statement of future intentions was ingested but no memory candidate was extracted, causing silent data loss. The reusable mechanism is omission of explicit future goals or aspirations during extraction. A skill that forces extraction of stated plans and desired outcomes transfers across any future-oriented intention statements, preventing the same ingestion-stage loss.

payload.name: Preserve_Explicit_Advice_During_Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, preserve explicit advice, recommendations, or instructions in content instead of summarizing a mixed message as generic support; use when a speaker gives concrete guidance alongside encouragement.
content: During candidate extraction, if a source message contains explicit advice, recommendations, or action steps, include that specific guidance in the candidate content; do not reduce the message to a generic emotional-support summary.
When a message mixes concrete instructions with encouragement, prioritize the actionable content so a future recall can retrieve what was advised, not just that support was offered.
When updating an existing memory, ensure the new content preserves or merges any concrete advice from the source and does not become more generic than the previous version.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an extraction candidate reduced a message containing concrete advice to a generic summary of encouragement, so future questions about the advice cannot be answered. The reusable mechanism is collapsing actionable guidance into vague support during memory extraction. This applies to any conversational message where a speaker gives explicit recommendations alongside emotional support; the skill ensures those recommendations are preserved in memory content.

payload.name: Extract explicit future plans as distinct memories
payload.description: When constructing memories, if a speaker states a future plan or joke in one message, ensure it is extracted as a distinct candidate and not merged with unrelated earlier statements from other turns.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit future intention, plan, or joke (e.g., 'Maybe I'll...', 'I might...'), extract it as its own candidate, preserving the specific activity and using memory_kind 'plan' for intentions or 'event' for jokes/hypotheticals.

Do not merge this statement with earlier unrelated reflections about the speaker's habits or thoughts; keep candidates scoped to the source message unless the content is explicitly connected by the speaker.
When in doubt, prefer a separate candidate over an incomplete merged one; a longer, accurate memory is better than a short one that omits a key claim.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because the extraction candidate merged a speaker's explicit future plan (writing a screenplay) with unrelated earlier reflections, omitting the plan. The generalizable mechanism is that extraction can conflate content across turns and drop key stated intentions. This skill applies whenever a message contains an explicit future intention or hypothetical activity; it directs the agent to keep such statements as separate, faithful memory candidates.

payload.name: Extract direct suggestions as memory candidates
payload.description: When a conversation contains a direct suggestion, recommendation, or encouragement from one speaker to another (e.g. 'Keep doing X', 'try Y'), use this skill during memory construction to ensure that advice is captured as a candidate and not skipped as non-factual.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit advice or suggestions as memory-worthy. If a speaker directly tells another participant to continue, try, or adopt an action ('Keep doing X', 'You should Y', 'Try Z'), do not skip the message because it is not a statement of current fact.

Record the speaker, the addressee, and the recommended action in the candidate (e.g., as a state or event memory). During CRUD, preserve such candidates as normal memory updates and do not discard them for being advice.

candidates.solves: Memory construction misses explicit suggestions and advice phrased as encouragement or second-person guidance, leaving later questions about recommendations unanswerable. The failure mechanism is skipping non-assertive speech acts during candidate extraction. This skill applies whenever one speaker directly tells another to keep doing, try, or adopt an action, and requires capturing that advice as a candidate.

payload.name: Extract Encouragement and Supportive Utterances
payload.description: When a speaker offers encouragement, sympathy, advice, or reassurance to another person, extract it as an event or relationship memory, including the key content and any linked setback.
content: During extraction, treat supportive, encouraging, or advising messages as memory-worthy events: record the speaker, the recipient, and the gist of the support/advice (e.g., 'X told Y that rejections don't define her, keep trying').
If the support references a prior setback or difficulty (explicit or implied), link this event to that existing state/event memory.
Also evaluate whether the utterance reveals a relationship quality (e.g., supportive, caring) and update or create a relationship memory between the participants when appropriate.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes fails to extract memories from messages that contain emotional support, encouragement, or advice, leaving such facts unpersisted and unanswerable later. This occurs because supportive utterances are not explicitly recognized as memory-worthy events or relationship cues. This skill applies whenever one participant offers reassurance, motivation, or guidance to another, especially after a setback or challenge, and guides extraction of the gist, the relationship signal, and any linked prior state.

payload.name: Extract suggestions and recommendations
payload.description: When a message contains one participant explicitly suggesting or recommending a specific item, resource, activity, or action to another participant, extract it as a memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly suggests or recommends a specific item (e.g., a book, resource, activity, action) to another participant, create a memory capturing the suggestion. Include the suggested item and the stated purpose or benefit if present. Store it as an event or relationship memory, evidence-bound and source-linked to the message. Do not skip such statements because they are phrased as advice rather than assertions.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an explicit suggestion or recommendation made by one participant to another was not extracted during candidate ingestion, leaving a gap for later questions about what someone suggested. The failure mechanism is a tendency to skip advisory statements as non-factual. A reusable rule to extract suggestions as event or relationship memories applies to any future conversation with explicit recommendations of items, resources, or actions, independent of topic.

payload.name: ExtractAdviceSuggestionsFromConversation
payload.description: When a speaker offers a suggestion, recommendation, or advice to another participant, use this skill to extract it as a memory candidate even if embedded or not accepted.
content: During candidate extraction, identify turns where one speaker advises, recommends, or suggests an action to another (e.g., 'consider X', 'maybe try Y'). Create a memory candidate for the suggestion even if it is part of a longer message and regardless of whether the recipient accepts it.

When storing the suggestion, prefer a 'plan' memory type if the suggested action is intended for the recipient; otherwise use 'preference' if it reflects the advisor's own preference. Record the advisor, recipient, and the advised action.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction missed a suggestion because it was embedded in a longer message and not accepted. The abstract mechanism is that advisory statements, especially those referring to a prior problem, are often not captured. This skill applies to future conversations where a participant gives a recommendation or advice to another; it does not apply to purely factual statements or exchanges without advisory intent.

payload.name: Preserve explicit process steps in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message that describes how to do something (care, maintenance, routine, procedure), preserve each concrete step/action in memory content; do not reduce the message to an evaluative summary or preference.
content: During extraction, if a message answers a how-to or process question by listing concrete actions (e.g., keep clean, feed properly, provide light), capture those actions as part of the memory content, not just an overall judgment like 'low-maintenance'.

When a speaker expresses an attitude about a task and then gives enumerated steps, extract the steps as separate factual details or include them explicitly in the same memory; the evaluative label alone is insufficient.
Use memory_kind and subject appropriate to the speaker; the concrete steps belong in the content regardless of whether they are framed as preference or routine.

candidates.solves: When a speaker answers a how-to or process question with an evaluative statement plus concrete steps (e.g., 'not tough; do X, do Y'), extraction often keeps only the evaluation and drops the steps. This skill requires preserving all explicit procedural steps in memory so later factual questions about the process can be answered.

payload.name: ExtractPlansFromInvitationReplies
payload.description: During extraction, use when a speaker replies to an invitation or question about future plans with concrete desired activities, even if tentative ('maybe we can', 'I'd love to').
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker responds to an invitation or a question about future plans by naming concrete activities they would like to do, create a plan candidate even if the message has no explicit date or commitment words.

Use 'plan' as the memory type for activities to be done together at a future visit or event; include the participants and the activity, and resolve relative times ('tomorrow', 'when I come over') from the message timestamp.
Do not skip such replies because they are conversational or tentative; 'maybe we can' or 'I'd love to' still expresses an intention worth persisting.

candidates.solves: When a speaker replies to an invitation or a question about upcoming plans by naming concrete activities they would like to do together, the Construction Agent sometimes fails to extract any candidate, so the plan is never persisted. This pattern occurs across any future-visit, meeting, or event dialogue whenever tentative or conversational phrasing still expresses a clear intention. The skill generalizes the need to treat such replies as plan candidates regardless of the specific activity, time, or participants.

payload.name: Verify existing coverage before skipping add candidate
payload.description: When a construction decision is about to SKIP an extracted fact with a reason like 'already included' or 'already in memory', verify against the retrieved memory pool and accepted changes before skipping.
content: Before choosing SKIP for an extracted candidate, verify that the fact is actually covered by a retrieved existing memory or by an earlier accepted ADD/UPDATE in the same batch. If no such memory or change exists, do not skip: ADD the candidate as a new memory.
Do not accept a SKIP reason such as 'Information already included in the updated memory' unless you can identify the specific memory ID or change event that contains the same fact.

candidates.solves: Construction SKIP can drop valid facts when the model assumes prior coverage ('already included') without checking the existing-memory pool or accepted batch changes. Apply whenever a candidate is about to be SKIPped as duplicate: confirm the fact exists in retrieved memories or earlier accepted updates. Not for cases with actual coverage or retrieval-side issues.

payload.name: Verify duplicate before skipping memory candidate
payload.description: When a Construction Agent is about to SKIP an extracted candidate because it appears duplicate, verify an equivalent memory actually exists in the retrieved related-memory pool before skipping. If no such memory is present, do not SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate on duplicate grounds, confirm that an equivalent memory is actually present in the retrieved related-memory pool or current snapshot version.
If no existing memory supports the claimed duplication, do not skip: ADD the candidate, or MERGE only when a concrete target memory exists.
A generic 'duplicate information already represented' reason is not sufficient when the related-memory pool is empty or contains no matching memory.

candidates.solves: During batched memory construction, a candidate can be marked as duplicate and skipped even when the related-memory pool contains no equivalent memory, so the fact is never persisted. This rule ensures duplicate checks compare against actually retrieved existing memories rather than inferred or generic duplication. It applies to future construction decisions where SKIP is considered for a new candidate and no matching memory is visible in the retrieved pool.

payload.name: Verify existing memory before SKIP decision
payload.description: When a construction candidate would be skipped as already represented, verify that a matching memory actually exists in the retrieved existing-memory pool before selecting SKIP; if no matching memory is found, choose ADD.
content: Before applying SKIP to a candidate with the reason 'already represented', explicitly search the retrieved existing-memory pool for a memory that covers the same subject, predicate, and key details.
If no such memory is found in the retrieved pool, do not SKIP the candidate; create it with ADD (or MERGE/UPDATE only if a partially related memory exists).
SKIP is only valid when the exact fact is demonstrably present in the visible memory pool; absence of the fact is not a reason to discard the candidate.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions sometimes skip adding a candidate because they assume the fact already exists in memory, even when the retrieved existing-memory pool contains no matching memory. This causes durable facts to be lost. The fix is a reusable rule: before choosing SKIP on the grounds that a candidate is already represented, the agent must confirm the matching memory is actually present in the retrieved pool; if it is absent, ADD the candidate. This applies to any future construction batch where a candidate seems redundant but the pool does not contain the corresponding memory.

payload.name: Verify actual redundancy before skipping candidate
payload.description: Use when deciding to SKIP a candidate as duplicate or redundant; if the related memory pool is empty or lacks the equivalent fact, persist the candidate instead.
content: Before skipping a candidate with reason 'duplicate or redundant', verify that a retrieved related memory explicitly contains the same subject and fact; an empty pool or a non-covering memory invalidates the skip.

When the related memory pool is empty or does not contain the equivalent fact, ADD the candidate (or MERGE into the closest existing memory if the fact is missing there) rather than skipping it. When uncertain, prefer persisting over dropping evidence.

candidates.solves: Construction sessions sometimes skip an ADD candidate as 'duplicate or redundant' without verifying that a related memory actually covers the fact, which loses evidence when the memory pool is empty. This rule requires confirming redundancy against the retrieved memory set and, when none exists, persisting the candidate to preserve the fact.

payload.name: Verify duplicate before SKIP in construction
payload.description: When a construction candidate is marked as a duplicate but no retrieved existing memory matches its subject and content, use this to require verification before SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate, confirm that an actually retrieved existing memory contains the same subject and fact; never assume duplication from prior conversation or memory. If the existing-memory pool has no matching memory, ADD the candidate as a new memory with the appropriate kind and source link.

candidates.solves: Prevents construction from dropping valid extracted facts by SKIPping them as duplicates when no retrieved existing memory actually contains the same information. Applies whenever a candidate is skipped on duplication grounds and the existing-memory pool is empty or lacks a matching memory.

payload.name: AddNewMemoryWhenNoExistingMatch
payload.description: When a candidate contains new, evidence-backed information and no existing memory is retrieved for merging, use ADD rather than SKIP.
content: During CRUD decisions, if no existing memory matches a candidate, do not skip it for that reason; issue an ADD operation to create a new memory.
Before deciding SKIP, confirm the candidate is redundant or unsupported; lack of an update/merge target alone is not a valid skip reason.
This applies to the CRUD decision stage; extraction should still produce candidates for all new facts regardless of existing memory.

candidates.solves: This addresses the pattern where a new, evidence-backed fact is dropped during CRUD because no existing memory matches. The rule applies to any candidate representing new information; it does not apply when the candidate is redundant, unsupported, or outside the allowed memory kinds.

payload.name: Verify Existing Memory Before Skip Already Included
payload.description: Use during construction CRUD decisions when a candidate is marked SKIP with the reason 'already included in the updated memory' or similar. Before skipping, confirm that a prior memory version or the current pool actually contains the fact; otherwise ADD the candidate.
content: Before deciding SKIP on an ADD candidate with reason 'already included in updated memory', check the retrieved existing-memory pool and prior versions for the same subject and fact. If no memory contains that information, do not skip; perform ADD to persist the extracted fact. Only SKIP when you can point to an existing memory version that genuinely includes the fact.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip a newly extracted fact as 'already included' even when no prior memory contains it, losing durable facts. The reusable rule is to verify the fact exists in the retrieved pool or prior versions before SKIPing for duplication; if not, ADD the candidate. Applies to any future construction CRUD decision where a SKIP reason claims existing coverage but no memory supports it.

payload.name: Confirm-Duplicate-Before-Skip
payload.description: Apply during construction when a memory candidate would be SKIPped because the information is already included; verify a real memory exists first.
content: Before choosing SKIP with reason 'information already included', identify the exact memory that already contains the candidate's fact: either an existing memory from the retrieved pool or a memory actually created earlier in the same batch.
If no such memory exists, do not SKIP the candidate; ADD it as a new memory.
When multiple candidates in the same batch are near-duplicates, create at least one memory from them instead of skipping all of them with the assumption that another candidate will be persisted.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes SKIP a memory candidate with the reason 'information already included' even when no prior memory exists and no memory is actually created, causing the fact to be lost. This Skill applies whenever a candidate is dismissed as a duplicate: it requires confirming a concrete existing or newly created memory before skipping, and otherwise forces an ADD. It generalizes to any CRUD decision where redundancy is assumed without evidence.

payload.name: CaptureExplicitReasonsInEventExtraction
payload.description: When a message states a reason, cause, or motivation for an action, include it in the event memory content during extraction.
content: During extraction, when the speaker states why an action occurred (e.g., 'because', 'so I did', 'I wanted to', 'saw X and had to'), include that reason in the event memory content rather than recording only the action or outcome.
During update/enrichment of an event memory, if any source message explicitly gives a reason or motivation for the event and it is missing, add it before adding unrelated details.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an extraction candidate recorded an action or event but omitted the explicitly stated reason or motivation for it, and later enrichment added unrelated details instead of filling that gap. This pattern occurs whenever a speaker explains why they did something and a future question asks 'why'. The rule generalizes to any event memory: capture stated reasons during extraction and verify they are present during updates.

payload.name: Preserve explicit subjective descriptors in experience memories
payload.description: When extracting or reviewing memories from an experiential statement, if the source explicitly states a feeling or uses an evaluative adjective, include that descriptor in the candidate or existing memory content.
content: When extracting or reviewing memories from an experiential statement, preserve any explicit subjective descriptors (feelings, evaluative adjectives like peaceful, amazing, scary) that appear in the source.
Do not invent or infer descriptors that are not explicitly stated; only preserve those present in the source.
During CRUD, if an existing memory misses an explicit descriptor from its source message, update the memory to include that descriptor.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly describes an experience with an evaluative adjective or feeling (e.g., peaceful, terrifying, amazing), extraction candidates that condense the event often drop that descriptor, leaving memory unable to answer later questions about how the speaker felt. This rule applies to any experiential statement during extraction and to existing memories that miss such explicit descriptors; it does not require inventing descriptors absent from the source.

payload.name: Preserve_explicit_activity_qualifiers
payload.description: When constructing memories from messages where a speaker describes an activity with explicit intensity or descriptive qualifiers (nonstop, futuristic, etc.), preserve those details in the extracted candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, when the source expresses an activity with explicit intensity, frequency, or descriptive context (e.g., 'nonstop', 'futuristic setting'), preserve those qualifiers in the memory content verbatim or in close paraphrase.
Do not collapse detailed activity descriptions into generic summaries like 'enjoyed it'; include the specific attributes that make the event distinct and that could be queried later.
If multiple activities share a message, keep each activity's distinctive qualifiers; avoid merging them into a single vague statement that loses per-activity detail.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage omitted salient qualifiers like 'nonstop' and 'futuristic setting/gameplay', storing a generic enjoyment summary. This rule instructs extractors to carry explicit intensity and context modifiers into memory content, preventing loss of queryable facts. It applies to any future session where an activity is described with such specific attributes.

payload.name: Capture all named participants' stated preferences in shared activities
payload.description: When a source message says a person or pet likes/enjoys an activity with others, use it during extraction before updating memories to record the preference for every named participant, not only the speaker's plan.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that a named subject (including a pet) loves/enjoys an activity with others, create or update memory so that subject's preference for that activity is represented.

Before performing an UPDATE that adds an activity to a memory, check the source sentence for all named participants who are said to enjoy it; include their enjoyment, not only the main subject's plans or general appreciation.
Apply this to activities such as walks, hikes, or other outings whenever the source attributes enthusiasm to multiple named individuals.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often paraphrase a shared-activity statement from only the speaker's perspective, dropping another named participant's stated preference (e.g., a pet that loves the activity), leaving later questions about that participant partially unsupported. This rule applies whenever source text explicitly attributes enjoyment of an activity to multiple named subjects; it does not apply to inferred or unstated preferences.

payload.name: Preserve explicit process descriptions in extracted memories
payload.description: During construction extraction, use when a speaker explicitly describes how an action was performed (process, manner, mood, or attitude); preserve that description in the memory rather than dropping it for a broader summary.
content: When a message contains an explicit description of how an action was performed or experienced (process, manner, mood, or attitude), preserve that description in the extracted memory; paraphrase the speaker's key phrases instead of dropping them in favor of a broader emotional summary.

When a speaker directly answers a question about the manner or process of an action, treat that answer as a distinct memory-worthy fact and ensure it is retained when merging related messages into one memory.

candidates.solves: During extraction, summaries of multi-message events often drop the speaker's explicit description of how an action was performed, retaining only broader emotional context; later questions about that process then lack evidence. Applies when a message or exchange directly states the manner, attitude, or process of an action; not when such details are only inferable.

payload.name: Extract explicit emotional appraisals as separate state memories
payload.description: Use during construction when a message contains an explicit emotional evaluation or appraisal about an event; extract the subjective feeling as a state memory in addition to any factual event memory.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly states an emotional evaluation or appraisal of an event (e.g., 'huge success', 'relief', 'thrilled'), create a state memory for that feeling with subject, emotion, and triggering event, in addition to any event memory.

During ADD/UPDATE, before persisting, verify that explicit emotional appraisals in the source are represented in candidate memories; if only the factual event is captured, add or update the state memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops explicit affective appraisals when an event is also present, leaving later state/feeling questions unanswered. This applies whenever a source message states both a factual occurrence and the speaker's explicit emotional evaluation of it; preserve the feeling as a state memory. Not for inferring unstated emotions.

payload.name: Preserve compound emotional states in extraction
payload.description: When a user's message expresses multiple or contrasting feelings about the same topic (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), use when extracting memory candidates to ensure all emotional components are retained.
content: During extraction, if a speaker expresses more than one distinct emotion or attitude toward the same subject in a single message, preserve all of them in the memory content. Do not drop one feeling to keep only the more positive, prominent, or recent one.
Pay special attention to contrastive structures such as 'X but Y', 'although X, Y', 'X yet Y', 'X still Y' — each side is an explicit claim and must appear in the extracted memory.
