If both feelings are about an ongoing search, plan, or state, either combine them in one event/state memory or create separate state memories; do not merge them into a single sentiment that omits one component.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly expresses contrasting or multiple feelings about the same subject in one utterance (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), extraction may preserve only the more salient or positive component, losing the other. This rule applies during candidate extraction: any explicitly stated emotion or attitude must be preserved, especially when linked by contrast words like 'but', 'although', 'yet', or 'still'. It does not apply to inferred emotions or single-emotion statements, and it is not a prompt to invent feelings not stated.

payload.name: Preserve activity purpose context in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message where a person describes an activity, hobby, or routine with a stated purpose, reason, or condition (e.g., to keep busy, while recovering), include that context in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a speaker describes an activity with a stated purpose, reason, or condition (e.g., 'to keep busy while healing', 'to relax after work'), preserve that context in the candidate content. Do not create a memory that states the activity alone; include the reason or circumstance because later questions often target it.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an activity extraction candidate omitted the speaker's stated purpose/condition (painting to keep busy while healing a knee), so the memory could not answer a later question about that purpose. The abstract mechanism is loss of purpose context during extraction. This Skill preserves such context so future sessions can answer why/when an activity occurred, when a message states an explicit reason or circumstance. It does not apply when no purpose is stated.

payload.name: Preserve first-person experiential claims in memory
payload.description: When a message states how an activity or object makes the speaker feel or connects them to someone, include that first-person experience in memory candidates and updates.
content: During extraction, if the speaker explicitly describes their own emotional response or an activity's felt meaning (e.g., 'it's like...', 'comforting', 'makes me feel connected'), create a candidate capturing that first-person experience rather than only a related belief or value.
During an UPDATE/MERGE, preserve or add such directly stated experiences; replacing a first-person feeling with a paraphrase of someone else's belief loses required memory content.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that extraction kept only another person's belief and omitted the speaker's own statement about how an activity feels and that it is comforting. This pattern recurs when construction paraphrases a related value or belief and drops the speaker's direct emotional/experiential claim, leaving memory unable to answer later questions. The rule applies to any future memory construction from first-person statements about feelings, comparisons, or felt connections; it does not apply to inferring unstated emotions.

payload.name: Preserve explicit emotional reactions in extracted memories
payload.description: During extraction, when a narrative includes an explicit feeling or significance statement after an event, keep that affective claim in the memory candidate instead of replacing it with a factual summary.
content: During candidate extraction, preserve the speaker's explicit emotional or evaluative statements (e.g., love, relief, gratitude, importance) when they are tied to a described event.

Do not collapse a narrative into only its factual action; include the expressed feeling as a separate memory or as part of the same memory so later questions about the speaker's reaction are answerable.

candidates.solves: When constructing memories from conversational narratives, extraction summaries can drop the speaker's explicit emotional reaction, leaving later questions about the speaker's feelings unsupported. This skill applies whenever a user tells a first-person anecdote that contains an explicit feeling or significance statement: preserve that affective claim rather than only summarizing the factual event.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitEmotionalReactions
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly describes how they felt about an event or achievement during memory extraction, create a state memory capturing that reaction instead of skipping the message.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly states a speaker's emotional reaction to an event or accomplishment, create a state memory capturing that reaction and its trigger. Do not discard the message merely because it contains no new factual event; encode the feeling as a state with source reference.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes skips messages that contain only an explicit emotional reaction to a personal milestone or accomplishment, leaving that reaction absent from memory. Future extractions should recognize such explicitly stated feelings as durable state facts and ingest them, regardless of the underlying topic.

payload.name: Preserve Explicitly Named Feelings in Extracted Memories
payload.description: When a user explicitly names feelings (e.g., peace, gratitude, joy) about a person, place, event, or memory, include those exact emotions in the extracted memory content instead of a vague summary.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states an emotion they feel (e.g., 'I feel peace and gratitude'), include those named feelings in the candidate memory content rather than replacing them with generic summaries like 'cherished memories' or 'feels connected'.

When writing or updating event/experience memories, preserve the speaker's exact emotional descriptors as evidence; a memory that records only a vague positive sentiment will fail later questions about specific feelings.
If multiple named emotions are given, list them explicitly; do not merge or omit any.

candidates.solves: This solves extraction candidates that paraphrase away explicitly stated emotions, making memories unable to answer later questions about the user's feelings. The diagnosed cause was an event memory that kept 'cherished memories' but dropped 'peace and gratitude' even though both were explicit in the source. The abstraction is to treat named emotions as core evidence to preserve verbatim. It applies to any future conversation where a speaker describes their emotional response to a person, place, shared experience, or memory.

payload.name: Preserve Affective Statements in Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, if a message contains explicit feelings or statements about how a person, pet, or activity affects the speaker, include those affective details in the candidate content rather than omitting them for other factual details.
content: During extraction, when a source message contains explicit emotional states or relationship evaluations (e.g., how a person, pet, or activity makes the speaker feel), keep those details in the candidate memory content even when the message also includes other factual information.

When updating or enriching an existing memory, if the new message adds an affective evaluation not yet stored, incorporate it into the updated content rather than only adding the more concrete factual elements.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates omitted explicit affective facts in favor of factual details, so memories lost how the speaker feels. The reusable rule is to preserve emotional/relationship-evaluative statements whenever a message mixes them with other information, so future questions about feelings can be answered. Applies to any message expressing how a person, pet, or activity affects the speaker; not needed when no such affective content exists.

payload.name: Extract explicit emotional reactions as state memories
payload.description: During memory extraction, if a message explicitly says how the person felt about an event, add a state/event memory for the emotion in addition to any plans; do not keep only future-oriented facts.
content: When extracting memories, first scan for explicit emotional reactions (e.g., 'thrilled', 'rewarding', 'felt appreciated') tied to an event.
For each explicit reaction, create a separate 'state' or 'event' memory capturing the feeling and the triggering event, even if the message also contains plans.
Do not omit emotional reactions merely because they are subjective or because a more actionable plan candidate exists in the same message.

candidates.solves: When a person explicitly states an emotional reaction (e.g., thrilled, rewarding) to an event, extraction often keeps only the following plans and drops the subjective reaction, making the memory incomplete. This rule ensures those reactions are stored as a state/event memory alongside any plans, so future questions about feelings can be answered.

payload.name: Extract-durable-joy-sources-alongside-transient-stress
payload.description: When a speaker mentions a temporary stressful situation and in the same message says what always cheers them up or brings them joy, extract both the transient state and the durable source of joy as separate memories.
content: During extraction, treat statements like 'X always cheers me up', 'watching X makes me so happy', or 'X brings me joy' as durable preference/relationship facts even when embedded in a sentence about a temporary problem.
Create a separate candidate for the enduring source of cheer/joy (e.g., a person, pet, hobby, or object) with memory kind preference or relationship, not only a candidate for the transient state.
Do not merge the durable fact into a stress/tournament event memory; keep the lasting preference/relationship distinct so it remains retrievable later.
If a single utterance contains both a situational event and a stable emotional resource, extract both; skipping one loses answerable information.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent extracted only a transient stress/tournament event from a message that also stated the speaker's turtles always cheer them up, so the durable, answerable preference was never persisted. This skill abstracts the failure: any utterance pairing a temporary situation with an explicit enduring source of cheer/joy should yield separate memories for the situational event and the durable preference/relationship. It applies to future conversations where people mention pets, hobbies, objects, or people as ongoing emotional resources while also describing a current difficulty.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitBehavioralReactions
payload.description: When a message states an explicit reaction/behavior of a person, pet, or group to a condition (e.g., hates snow, confused by snow), extract it as a standalone memory fact during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit reaction, emotion, or behavior of a subject (person, pet, or group) to a specific condition or event, create a separate memory for that reaction (e.g., memory kind 'state' or 'event') rather than merging it into a broader attribute or preference summary.

When updating an existing memory with new information, preserve previously captured explicit reactions; do not overwrite them with a general preference unless the new source explicitly contradicts the earlier reaction.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a message was summarized into a general preference statement, omitting an explicitly stated behavioral reaction ('dogs hate snow and were confused'). The mechanism is that multiple distinct facts in one message get collapsed into a single enrichment, losing the specific reaction needed to answer future questions. This skill applies whenever a source message contains an explicit reaction or behavior of an entity to a condition, and that reaction must be preserved as its own memory fact.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitCopingMechanisms
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that something helps them cope, distract, or feel better during difficult times, extract it as a preference memory.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly says an activity, pet, hobby, or person helps the user cope, stay distracted, or feel better when times are tough, create a preference memory that captures the coping mechanism and its stated purpose.

candidates.solves: The construction failed because no candidate was generated from a message explicitly naming coping mechanisms (a pet and an activity) that help during tough times. The abstract mechanism is that extraction often ignores explicit statements about what comforts or distracts the user. This Skill adds a reusable extraction rule for such explicit coping mentions, transferring across topics and preventing future omissions of directly stated preferences.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitSentimentInExtraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, if a message contains an explicit evaluation or sentiment about something, preserve that evaluative claim along with any descriptive details.
content: During extraction, when the source message includes an explicit evaluation or sentiment about a person, entity, or event (e.g., positive/negative judgment, like/dislike, satisfaction), include that evaluation in the candidate content. Do not drop it just because you also capture descriptive attributes.
Before finalizing an extraction candidate, check that every independent evaluative claim in the message is represented; if any is missing, add the missing claim.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes preserve descriptive details while dropping a speaker's short explicit sentiment, causing partial memories for later opinion questions. The rule to include every explicit evaluative claim in candidate content fixes this mechanism and transfers across domains. It applies when a message states a reaction or judgment; not to purely factual summaries without sentiment.

payload.name: Preserve concrete activity tied to a stated feeling
payload.description: When extracting during construction, if the speaker explicitly links a specific activity or behavior to a feeling or experience, include that concrete activity in the memory rather than only the emotion or a general summary.
content: During extraction, when a message states that a specific activity or behavior caused or enabled a feeling (e.g., freeing, magical, peaceful, fun), record the concrete activity together with the feeling in the memory content; do not replace the activity with a general description of the event.
Apply before finalizing event or state memories so later questions about what specifically produced the feeling can be answered from the stored memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the emotional summary of an experience and drops the specific activity the speaker explicitly tied to that feeling, making the memory unable to answer later questions about what was freeing, enjoyable, peaceful, etc. This rule applies whenever a narrative pairs a concrete action with a stated feeling, and requires preserving that action alongside the feeling. It is not meant to force verbatim inclusion of every detail, only the activity that is the direct object of the stated feeling.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-reported states during construction
payload.description: When a person directly states a current condition or experience (e.g., stress, health, emotion) in any message turn, use this to create a state memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, identify explicit self-reported states from any message turn, even if the statement is brief or embedded in social chat. Examples include 'dealing with work stress', 'feeling sick', or 'really busy with exams'.

Create a `state` memory candidate for the speaker: include the condition, the time implied by the message timestamp, and any qualifier (e.g., work-related). Do not wait for a later follow-up before recording the state.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes ignore explicit statements about a person's current condition when they appear as brief side remarks in casual conversation, so later questions about that condition cannot be answered from memory. This skill applies whenever a speaker directly reports experiencing stress, illness, mood, workload, or similar states, and requires extracting it as a state memory candidate with the reported time.

payload.name: Preserve explicit entity descriptions in memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories, if a message explicitly describes or evaluates an entity with a specific adjective or phrase, retain that specific quality instead of only capturing general sentiment.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly describes or evaluates an entity with a specific quality (adjective or phrase), preserve that quality in the memory content (e.g., 'Gina described the studio as amazing').

Do not replace the explicit descriptive term with a generic emotion like excitement or support. Keep the subject-attribute relationship visible so future recall can answer 'how' or 'what' questions about the entity.

candidates.solves: The construction agent omitted an explicit descriptive adjective ('amazing') from an extracted memory, replacing it with generic excitement. This rule fixes the general mechanism of collapsing direct evaluative statements into vague sentiment, which loses queryable attributes. It applies to any extraction where a message contains a clear description/evaluation of a person, place, or object that could be asked about later.

payload.name: Extract implicit preferences from love/passion statements
payload.description: When a message includes an emotional expression like 'doing what I love', 'I enjoy', or 'my passion' about an activity, and the activity is identifiable from nearby context, create a separate preference memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, identify statements where the speaker expresses an affective attitude (love, enjoy, passion, pride) toward an activity. Resolve the activity from the same or immediately preceding clauses (e.g., 'competing in tournaments').
Create a separate `preference` memory capturing that the subject likes/loves that activity, with the activity as the object, rather than only embedding it in an event memory.
If the activity is already represented in an event candidate, still add the preference memory; do not merge it into the event content.

candidates.solves: When a message contains an affective statement about an activity (e.g., 'doing what I love', 'I enjoy it', 'it's my passion'), extraction often records only the factual event and misses the implied preference. This skill applies to any future message where a speaker expresses love, enjoyment, or pride toward an identifiable activity; it instructs creating a separate preference memory for that activity, independent of any event memory. It does not apply when the activity cannot be resolved from context or the emotion is not directed at a specific activity.

payload.name: Preserve actor and precise object in interpersonal event extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a statement about an interpersonal action (mocking, teasing, criticizing, praising, blaming, etc.), use this to keep the actor(s) and the exact subject or reason in the memory content.
content: During extraction, for any clause describing an interpersonal action, retain who performed the action and the precise object or reason (e.g., 'friends mocked him for being overweight'), rather than compressing it to a vaguer form like 'he was mocked about his weight'.
Preserve these event modifiers even if the memory also records a response or decision; the actor and exact reason are independently queryable facts and must not be dropped.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred during extraction when an interpersonal event was summarized without preserving the actor(s) and the exact object or reason of the action, so later questions about who did something or what it was specifically about could not be answered. The reusable rule is to keep full attribution and precise modifiers for interpersonal events in extracted memories, regardless of the topic; this applies whenever a source statement describes someone mocking, criticizing, praising, blaming, or otherwise acting toward someone else.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitlyNamedEmotions
payload.description: When a message explicitly names a person's emotions about an event, plan, or outcome, include those emotions in the extracted memory and keep them in later updates.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly lists or names emotions (e.g., relief, excitement, anxiety, hope, worry) about an event or plan, capture those emotions in the candidate content instead of mentioning only the action or outcome.

During updates and enrichment, preserve explicitly stated emotions from earlier messages unless a later message directly contradicts them; do not replace specific emotions with a vague summary such as 'mixed emotions'.

candidates.solves: During construction, extraction candidates often capture actions and plans but omit explicitly stated emotions, and later enrichment can replace specific feelings with vague summaries, losing answerable claims. This skill ensures that when a speaker explicitly names emotions about an event or plan, those emotions are preserved as memory content during extraction and maintained through updates. It applies to any future conversation where a person articulates discrete feelings; it does not cover inferring unstated emotions.

payload.name: Capture-activity-origin-facts
payload.description: When a user explains how someone got into an activity, interest, or hobby (e.g., who introduced them, what inspired them), extract and preserve those origin facts instead of only a generic preference.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explains how they started an activity (e.g., 'my friend got me into it', 'it all started when...'), create a memory recording the origin: who/what introduced them, any gift or advice, and what inspired them.

Do not reduce such a message to only a generic current-state preference (e.g., 'enjoys X'); preserve the causal origin facts as a separate or enriched memory. When updating an existing memory, also add these origin facts if present in the source evidence.

candidates.solves: The construction agent collapsed an explicit origin story into a generic current-state preference, dropping the person, gift, advice, and inspiration that caused the activity. This rule makes extraction preserve causal origin facts whenever anyone recounts how they began a hobby or interest, so later questions about that origin can be answered from memory. It generalizes beyond painting to any activity origin narrative.

payload.name: Extract inspiration-source memories for creative projects
payload.description: When a speaker states that a specific source (place, person, event, experience, book) inspired or sparked ideas for a current or future creative work, extract a candidate memory.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit inspiration attributions as memory-worthy: if a speaker says a place, person, event, book, or experience 'sparked ideas', 'inspired', or 'got me thinking' about a current or future creative work, create a candidate memory capturing the work and the source.

Store it as a state memory in the form '[Speaker]'s [creative work] is inspired by [source]' (or equivalent), resolve relative time from the message timestamp, and link the source message. Do not skip because the work is not yet finished or named.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was that extraction produced no candidate for a clear inspiration statement, so a durable fact never entered memory. The reusable failure mechanism is that explicit attributions of inspiration for a creative project are often treated as casual chatter. This rule applies to any future session where a speaker attributes inspiration for a planned or ongoing creative work to a specific source, regardless of topic.

payload.name: ExtractOriginEventsForLongTermActivities
payload.description: When a message contains an origin story for a long-term activity (who introduced, age, first step) alongside a broader summary, extract the origin as a separate durable event and preserve it in later memory updates.
content: During extraction, if a speaker recounts how they began a long-term activity (e.g., who introduced them, at what age, the first concrete step), create a separate specific event candidate for that origin even when the message also summarizes later achievements.

During CRUD, when creating or updating a memory about a person's involvement in an activity, ensure any explicit origin details from the source message (initiator, age/time, starting action) are present; if missing, add or update a memory to include them.

candidates.solves: Extraction omissions occur when a speaker narrates how they began a long-term activity but the model creates only a broad summary memory, losing the specific origin event (who initiated, at what age, the first step). This skill forces extraction and CRUD to preserve origin details as a distinct durable fact, applying to any autobiographical narrative about starting a hobby, sport, career, or relationship. It does not apply when no origin is described or when the origin is already captured.

payload.name: preserve_explicit_origin_in_extracted_memories
payload.description: When constructing memories from statements that explicitly explain how an interest, hobby, skill, habit, or situation began, include the stated cause or origin in the memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if the source explicitly names who introduced, triggered, or advised the start of a hobby, interest, skill, habit, or situation, capture that causal detail in the candidate content, not only the resulting state or preference.
When the extracted memory already exists or overlaps, use UPDATE or MERGE to add the missing origin detail instead of creating a separate vague preference.
Do not infer an origin that is not explicitly stated; only preserve causes present in the evidence.

candidates.solves: During construction extraction, when a speaker explicitly states how an interest, hobby, skill, or situation began—including who introduced it, what triggered it, or what advice started it—the memory candidate often records only the resulting state or preference and drops the origin. This failure pattern is general across hobbies, roles, habits, and life events. The skill applies to extraction of explicitly stated causal origins, not to inferring causes that were not mentioned or to answer generation.

payload.name: Extract_Stated_Motivation_Drivers
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly names what motivates or drives them/their group to improve, extract a memory during ingestion.
content: During extraction, identify statements where a speaker explicitly names a motivating factor or driver (e.g., 'X drives us to...', 'that's what motivates me to...').
Create a compact memory candidate capturing the motivating factor and the speaker/group it applies to, using an existing memory type such as state or preference, linked to the source message.
Do not require the word 'motivate'; recognize causal phrasing like 'what drives us to get better.'

candidates.solves: The construction agent often misses explicit motivational-cause statements like 'X drives us to get better,' leaving the memory unable to answer 'what motivates [person]?' This skill adds a reusable extraction rule: during ingestion, treat explicit motivation/driver clauses as candidate memories tied to the speaker, applicable to any future conversation where a user states a cause for continued effort.

payload.name: ExtractCreationInspirationMemory
payload.description: When a user explicitly states what inspired or motivated them to create a drawing, character, story, or other work, extract that purpose as a memory during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker directly answers a question about inspiration, purpose, or motivation for creating something, extract a memory that captures both the creative item and the stated reason. Do not skip because the reason is subjective, visual, or internal.
Record the reason as a state or preference memory tied to the creative activity, preserving the speaker's own wording as evidence for future retrieval.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes omits memories when a speaker explains the purpose or inspiration behind a creative work, even though that explanation is a durable fact. This skill tells the extractor to treat such direct motivation statements as memory-worthy and capture them with the work they describe, so future questions about 'why' or 'what inspired' can be answered.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitMotivationWhenExtracting
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a reason or motivation that keeps them doing an activity, include that specific motivational fact during extraction and preserve it when updating existing memories.
content: During extraction, if the user explicitly states what motivates them or keeps them going in an activity, capture that explicit reason as part of the memory candidate instead of only summarizing emotional effects.
When updating an existing memory, do not discard previously stored explicit motivational facts unless the new message directly contradicts them.

candidates.solves: Failure: extraction summarized emotional benefits but omitted the speaker's explicit motivational reason, and a later update overwrote it. Reusable mechanism: explicit motivational/causal statements are lost during extraction/update. Apply when a user states what motivates or keeps them going; retain that specific reason in candidates and preserve stored motivational facts unless contradicted.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Frequency From How-Often Answers
payload.description: When a user directly answers how often they do an activity, extract a memory recording that activity and frequency, even if the answer is casual or includes extra reasons.
content: During candidate extraction, treat direct answers to 'how often' questions as memory-worthy facts even when phrased casually or embedded in small talk.

When the answer contains an explicit frequency (e.g., 'very often', 'multiple times a day', 'daily'), create a memory that records the activity and frequency; do not skip it because the user also gives reasons or benefits.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was ingestion: no candidate was generated from an explicit answer to a how-often question, so the fact never entered memory. The reusable mechanism is that direct frequency answers can be overlooked when expressed conversationally. This skill applies to any future construction pass where a user states how often an activity occurs; it does not apply to statements without explicit frequency or non-frequency topics.

payload.name: Extract past shared activity memories
payload.description: When a user describes a past activity done with a specific person and says it helped them bond or make memories, extract a candidate memory before continuing construction.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a past activity done with a specific person and explicitly says it helped them bond or make memories, create a candidate capturing the activity and the relationship context.
When processing such a message, do not skip candidate generation merely because the activity is mentioned in passing or as a reminiscence; treat it as a durable memory.
Use the session timestamp to place the activity in the past and store it as an event or relationship memory with the persons involved.

candidates.solves: Construction often drops memory-worthy recollections when a user briefly mentions a past shared activity and explicitly frames it as bonding or memory-making. This skill instructs extraction to generate a candidate for such statements instead of treating them as non-factual chatter, and to persist the activity with relationship context and a past timestamp.

payload.name: ExtractCompletedProjectEvent
payload.description: When a speaker states they finished or completed a project, task, or activity with a time reference, create an event memory for that speaker during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message contains a first-person statement about completing a project, task, or activity (e.g., 'finished X', 'completed X'), create an event memory for the speaker with the activity as the object.

Resolve relative time references (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday') against the message timestamp; if the exact date is uncertain, record the most precise resolution available (e.g., 'around' or 'before' the session date).
Use the 'event' memory kind for completed actions, not 'preference' or 'state'; preserve the speaker's attribute and any relevant context (e.g., effort or outcome).

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes skips creating a memory when a speaker explicitly states a completed action (e.g., finishing a project) because the base extraction prompt does not emphasize time-bound accomplishments. This skill adds a concrete extraction rule for such statements, resolving relative time from the session timestamp. It applies to any future message where a user mentions finishing or completing a tangible task or project, and is not meant for ongoing states, preferences, or unconfirmed intentions.

payload.name: Preserve-exact-time-and-quantity-wording
payload.description: When a source message contains vague temporal or quantity phrases (a few, several, a couple, etc.), use this to ensure memories keep the original wording unchanged.
content: When extracting memory candidates, copy temporal and quantity expressions (e.g., 'a few', 'several', 'a couple') exactly as they appear in the source message; do not paraphrase them into similar-sounding terms that change the meaning.

candidates.solves: A construction extraction error occurred when a memory candidate paraphrased 'a few years ago' into 'several years ago', altering the factual nuance. The failure mechanism is the loss of precision in paraphrasing approximate time/quantity expressions. This skill applies to any future construction extraction task where preserving the exact source wording of such quantifiers is required for evidence fidelity.

payload.name: Extract Activity Mentions from Casual Side Remarks
payload.description: When extracting candidate memories, if the target person mentions a concrete activity even briefly, create a candidate with companion and timing.
content: During candidate extraction, treat the target person's own statements as evidence regardless of message role.
Extract any concrete activity they say they do, did, or will do (e.g., hiking, walking, classes) even if it is a brief side remark or sign-off.
Record the activity and any named companion/participant. Use 'event' for one-time or upcoming actions and 'state' for recurring habits or preferences.
Do not skip a candidate because the surrounding message is mostly about another topic; a single explicit statement is sufficient.

candidates.solves: Construction ingestion omitted explicit activity claims because they appeared in brief side remarks or sign-offs. This skill makes extraction robust to casual placement: any concrete activity mentioned by the target person becomes a candidate, even if it is not the main topic. It applies to future sessions with activity statements embedded in small talk, across any topic.

payload.name: Capture all explicit facts during extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a user message, use this to avoid omitting explicit events or experiences that are not the dominant topic. Apply before finalizing candidates.
content: During extraction, after drafting candidates from a message, replay the message and verify that every explicit factual claim (who did what, when, where) is covered by at least one candidate. Do not omit a fact just because it is not the main topic or does not fit an existing memory's theme.
When a claim includes a relative time phrase such as 'last week' or 'yesterday', resolve it using the message/session timestamp and include the resolved date in the candidate's world_start.

candidates.solves: When a user message contains several explicit facts but one topic dominates the conversation, the extractor may silently drop a distinct stated event or experience because it does not fit the existing memory's theme. This skill requires the extractor to account for every explicit factual claim, including minor or unrelated anecdotes, and to resolve relative time references so that future questions about any stated fact can be answered from memory.

payload.name: Resolve-subject-before-extracting-availability
payload.description: When extracting memories from messages about meeting cancellations, reschedules, plans, or availability, use this to ensure the memory subject is the person who actually has the conflict or free time.
content: Before extracting a scheduling fact, identify the message speaker and resolve first-person pronouns; use that person as the subject for stated plans, conflicts, or free time.
Do not transfer a participant's stated plans or inability to the other participant unless a later message explicitly says the other has the same constraint.
When proposing an alternative time, a participant's 'I am free' only supports that participant's availability; do not assign it to the other participant without confirmation.
Applies during extraction and during any follow-up update/merge to avoid keeping a candidate with the wrong subject.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can assign a schedule conflict or availability to the wrong participant when a speaker mentions plans or free time. The diagnosed cause is a subject error during candidate generation. This skill requires resolving speaker and pronominal references before choosing a memory subject, and applies to cancellations, reschedules, or availability statements. It does not apply when the speaker explicitly refers to another person's schedule.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitNamedDetailsFromDirectAnswers
payload.description: Use during memory extraction when a user's reply to a question includes a named piece, title, work, or other specific entity that references a previous event; extract it as an event memory instead of skipping it.
content: During extraction, if the current user message directly answers a prior question about an event, performance, or achievement by naming a specific piece, title, work, or entity, create an event memory that records the speaker, the named detail, and the relevant context (e.g., the event it belongs to).
Do not skip a message just because it is brief or conversational; treat an explicit named detail provided in response to a question as a memory candidate.
Retain the named title or work verbatim in the event memory; do not paraphrase or replace it with a generic label.

candidates.solves: When a user answers a direct follow-up question about a past achievement or event by naming a specific piece, title, or work, the construction agent may fail to extract any memory, leaving the detail unpreserved. This rule ensures explicit named details stated in conversational answers are captured as event memories, and applies to any future multi-turn dialogue where a named entity is given in reply to a question.

payload.name: Capture_Completed_Project_Events
payload.description: Use during construction when a person mentions finishing or completing a specific project, task, or milestone in any message, even briefly or amid social chat.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly states they finished or completed a specific project, task, or milestone, create an event memory for it even if the message is otherwise social or the mention is brief.

During CRUD, ADD such event candidates; do not skip them because the source message was not primarily about the project. Resolve relative completion times (e.g., 'last week') from the message timestamp.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent omitted an explicit statement about a finished project when the message was mostly social. The failure is treating completion mentions as incidental unless the message is project-focused. Future conversations with passing or brief mentions of completed projects or milestones should still yield durable event memories. This applies to any speaker and project type; it does not cover extracting relationships, preferences, or other non-project facts.

payload.name: Extract all enumerated activities
payload.description: When extracting construction memories from a message where the speaker lists multiple distinct activities, experiences, or facts in one utterance, use this skill to ensure each listed item is captured.
content: During extraction, when a single user message enumerates multiple distinct activities or facts (e.g., studying, attending workshops, networking, presenting), create a memory candidate for each distinct item rather than only the most prominent or recent one.

Before adding an event memory that describes what someone did, scan the full source message for explicit lists and include every listed activity; if the activities are independent, prefer separate candidates so no listed fact is lost.

candidates.solves: Candidate extraction captured only the most salient activity from a message that explicitly enumerated several activities (studying, workshops, networking, presenting), so omitted facts were never stored. This pattern recurs when a single speaker message lists multiple distinct activities; extracting each enumerated item separately prevents incomplete memories. Applies to extraction of explicit lists, not to inferring unstated activities or merging existing memories.

payload.name: Preserve explicit outcomes in memory extraction
payload.description: Use when constructing memories from messages that state a specific achievement or result, ensuring the concrete outcome is retained rather than replaced by a generic summary.
content: During extraction, if the source explicitly states that someone achieved a specific outcome (e.g., 'reached their goals', 'won a competition'), include that concrete achievement in the memory content. Do not let a broader paraphrase (e.g., 'saw their growth') replace the explicitly mentioned result.

candidates.solves: When drafting a memory from an utterance, the model often over-summarizes explicitly stated concrete outcomes into vague terms, losing the fact needed for later questions. This rule applies to any extraction where the speaker mentions a specific achievement or result; it is not for unsupported inferences or implied outcomes.

payload.name: Preserve ordinal and temporal cues for creative works
payload.description: When extracting memories about a user's creative work (e.g., screenplay, book, art) and the conversation includes an ordinal like 'third' or a date/time reference, include both the ordinal and the inferred event date in the memory.
content: During extraction from messages about creative projects, if the speaker references an ordinal (first, second, third, etc.) or a start/completion time, record that ordinal as part of the artifact's identity and set the event's world_start to the message date when it indicates the start.
When adding or updating a creative-work memory, include the ordinal (e.g., 'third screenplay') in the content; do not summarize it away into a generic activity statement.

If the user confirms an ordinal in a reply (e.g., 'Yep! ...'), treat the confirmation as explicit evidence and encode it in the same event or profile memory, along with the date context from the session.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline sometimes summarizes creative-work discussions into generic profile/event memories, dropping ordinal identifiers (e.g., 'third', 'second') and concrete temporal references that are explicitly stated or contextually grounded in the conversation. This rule applies whenever a user mentions completing or working on a creative artifact with an ordinal or time cue; the memory should capture the ordinal and, if the surrounding session provides a date, that date as the work's start or completion time. It is not meant for cases where the ordinal or time is absent or ambiguous.

payload.name: Preserve source or discovery details in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a user message, if the message states how a person heard about or discovered an event, keep that detail in a memory.
content: When building memory candidates from a message, treat how the person learned about or discovered an event (e.g., saw a flyer, heard from a friend, read an ad) as a durable fact. Include it in the event memory or create a separate memory for it, even when the main action is something else. Do not drop this detail during extraction or later updates.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a message states how the person learned about or discovered an event (e.g., saw a flyer, heard from a friend, read an ad), that detail is often omitted when the main action is captured, so later questions like "how did X hear about Y?" cannot be answered. Preserving source/discovery details as part of the event memory or as a separate memory generalizes across workshops, classes, sales, and announcements; it does not require storing transient or non-durable context.

payload.name: Extract_Multiple_Facts_Per_Message
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a user message contains multiple distinct events, facts, or state changes; create a separate candidate for each rather than only the most salient one.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each explicit durable fact or event in a message as a separate candidate; do not let one salient topic (e.g., a trip) suppress another explicitly stated fact (e.g., a vehicle breakdown).
If a message contrasts two items or time periods (old vs new, before vs after), capture each side's state separately so that later questions can retrieve either fact.
Before finalizing a memory for a message, scan the raw text for every independent claim about the subject's possessions, plans, or experiences and ensure each is represented in some candidate.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was that extraction produced one candidate from a message containing two distinct user facts: a trip and a separate breakdown of a different item, so the breakdown was never stored. The abstract failure is single-candidate dominance, where a more prominent event causes other explicit durable facts in the same message to be omitted. This rule applies to any construction session where a message bundles multiple independent facts, events, or state changes, and prevents loss of evidence needed for later questions.

payload.name: Extract explicit relationship duration statements
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a speaker states an explicit duration for a relationship or group membership, generate a relationship memory candidate even if the statement is conversational.
content: During candidate extraction, identify explicit duration phrases attached to relationship or group-membership predicates, such as 'were teammates for X years', 'worked together since Y', or 'have known each other for Z years'.

For each identified phrase, create a relationship-type candidate memory that records the relationship and its stated duration; do not skip it because the sentence also contains conversational filler or a return question.
If the duration is given relative to a time mentioned in the message/session, resolve it to the session timestamp before finalizing the candidate.

candidates.solves: The construction run skipped extraction of a clear relationship-duration statement, leaving no memory to answer later questions. The reusable mechanism is that explicit durations attached to relationships are easy to overlook in conversational replies. This rule applies whenever a speaker states how long a relationship or group membership lasted; it does not apply when duration is only implied or must be inferred from context.

payload.name: Preserve explicit life-stage and duration facts
payload.description: When a message describes a person's history across explicit stages (schools, teams, careers) or states a duration, use specific stage/duration facts in memory extraction instead of a vague summary.
content: During extraction, identify explicit life-stage or level mentions (e.g., middle school, high school, college, professional) and duration phrases (e.g., for four years) in the source message.
Extract each such stage and duration as separate, memory-worthy facts; do not merge them into a generic phrase like 'since childhood.'
If a later message adds a stage or duration for the same topic, add or update the corresponding fact rather than relying on prior summary.

candidates.solves: A memory extraction often fails when a person's narrative is summarized as a general trajectory (e.g., played since childhood) and explicit educational or team stages and durations are dropped. This skill enforces extracting each explicit stage (middle school, high school, college, professional) and stated duration as separate durable facts. It applies to any future construction pass over biographical timeline statements in conversations, but does not infer stages or durations that are not explicitly stated.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Advice as Preference Memory
payload.description: Use during candidate extraction when a participant explicitly gives advice, recommendations, or criteria in response to another participant's question.
content: When extracting candidates from a session, treat explicit advice, recommendations, or criteria given by one participant to another as preference candidates, even if the advice is not about the speaker's own current plans or events.
Store the core advice compactly as a preference memory attributed to the advice-giver, and link it to the source message.
This rule applies only to candidate extraction; it does not require a separate CRUD operation and does not apply to casual or non-advice remarks.

candidates.solves: Explicit advice messages are ingested without producing a memory candidate, so guidance is lost. The mechanism is overlooking recommendation statements during extraction when they are not about the speaker's own plans/events. This applies when one participant gives advice or criteria to another; do not apply to non-advice casual remarks. Extract the core guidance as a preference memory attributed to the speaker and linked to the source message.

payload.name: Extract first-person explanatory preferences and states
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about why they made a choice or how they feel about something, extract the stated reason/preference/state as a memory candidate even if it lacks explicit preference wording.
content: During extraction, treat direct first-person answers to 'why' or feeling questions as evidence of durable preference or state.
Create a `preference` candidate for stated likes, choices, or motivations; create a `state` candidate for current feelings or conditions.
Do not require phrases like 'I like' or 'I prefer'; explanatory wording is sufficient.
Ensure the candidate is source-linked to the message.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: no candidate memory was created when a speaker directly explained her reason for a decision, leaving durable preference facts absent. The failure mechanism is extraction omitting first-person explanatory statements that convey preferences or states when not phrased as 'I like'. This applies to future answers that explain motivations, feelings, or choices; it does not apply to third-party descriptions, hypotheticals, or already-covered facts.

payload.name: Extract colloquial preference and activity statements as memory candidates
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a speaker uses informal positive/negative language (e.g., 'go crazy for', 'love', 'hate') to state a preference or activity, create a candidate even if the phrasing is not formal.
content: During candidate extraction, treat colloquial statements of preference or activity as explicit candidates. Phrases like 'go crazy for', 'love', 'hate', 'can't stand', 'prefer', or 'enjoy' signal durable likes, dislikes, or recurring activities.

Extract the subject, the liked/disliked item or activity, and any relevant context (such as location or time) into a compact preference/event candidate, even if the sentence is casual or conversational.
Do not skip extraction solely because the statement is informal or appears in a chatty reply; explicit sentiment about an entity is still a memory-worthy fact.

candidates.solves: Users often state stable preferences or activities informally ('go crazy for', 'love', 'hate'); extraction may skip these because wording is casual, so the fact never enters memory. Apply whenever a speaker explicitly expresses positive/negative preference or recurring activity, regardless of tone, during candidate extraction. This transfers across pets, people, foods, hobbies, and similar preference topics.

payload.name: Extract explicit preference statements
payload.description: When a participant explicitly states what they find beautiful, like, love, or prefer, create a `preference` candidate during extraction even if the statement appears inside a suggestion or plan.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly evaluates an entity positively (e.g., 'X is beautiful', 'I love Y'), create a `preference` candidate with the speaker as subject and the entity as object.
Do not skip the evaluation because it is embedded in a suggestion or plan (e.g., 'How about going there? The colors are so beautiful!'); the evaluative clause is still a durable preference.

candidates.solves: The failed fact was an explicit preference statement embedded in a suggestion, skipped at ingestion because it read as planning language. The reusable mechanism: evaluative clauses inside casual suggestion or plan wording still express the speaker's preference and must be extracted. Applies when a participant states what they find beautiful, like, love, or prefer; not to hypothetical conditionals or generic statements without an asserted preference.

payload.name: ExtractPreferencesFromAffectiveEndorsements
payload.description: When a speaker answers a direct question about a favorite or preference using positive evaluative language (e.g., 'really speaks to me', 'so expressive', 'love it') instead of explicit 'my favorite is', extract the endorsed item as a preference memory.
content: During candidate extraction, treat a first-person response to a favorite/preference question as a preference candidate even if it lacks the phrase 'favorite'; phrases like 'really speaks to me', 'I love', or 'so expressive' are sufficient evidence when they directly follow such a question.
Create a preference/profile memory for the endorsed entity with the speaker as the subject; do not wait for an explicit 'my favorite is X' formulation.
Do not apply to statements about others' preferences, hypothetical likes/dislikes, or mere mentions of an activity without affective endorsement.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline missed a durable preference memory because it required explicit 'favorite' wording and ignored affective endorsements given as direct answers to preference questions. This skill teaches extraction to recognize first-person evaluative responses as preference evidence, preventing missing profile memories across any domain whenever such responses occur.

payload.name: Include all explicit reasons in preference extraction
payload.description: When extracting a profile or preference memory, if the source explicitly gives multiple reasons for liking, disliking, or choosing something, include all distinct reasons in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly lists multiple reasons or traits for a preference or choice, capture every distinct reason in the candidate memory content; do not drop any reason because another reason seems more salient.
Before adding or updating a profile/preference memory, check the source message for every stated reason and ensure the memory content reflects all of them.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage sometimes records only a subset of explicitly stated reasons for a preference, so later questions about omitted reasons cannot be answered from memory. This rule applies whenever a source message lists multiple distinct reasons or traits for a like/dislike or choice: the extracted profile memory must include every explicit reason.

payload.name: Extract explicit stated preferences from conversational replies
payload.description: When a user explicitly names an item they like or calls it a favorite, during extraction create a preference/event candidate even if the statement is an enthusiastic answer to a question or uses informal wording.
content: During extraction, treat direct, unambiguous statements of liking or preference (e.g., 'X is my favorite', 'I love X', 'Definitely X!') as candidates for a preference memory, or an event memory when tied to a specific occasion, regardless of whether they occur in response to a question or in a casual/emphatic tone.

If the user names a specific item as their favorite, record it as its own candidate rather than embedding it only inside a broader summary, so future queries about that item can be answered from memory.
Do not skip a candidate solely because the mention is brief, colloquial, or part of a conversation about other topics.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes omits an explicit user statement of liking because it is phrased as a casual or emphatic reply to a question, causing later queries about that item to remain unanswered. This Skill ensures direct, unambiguous preference statements are always extracted as preference or event candidates, independent of the topic, so future questions about any named liked item are answerable.

payload.name: Extract explicit first-person preference statements as preference memories
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states a personal preference, favorite item, or like/dislike, use this during extraction to create a preference memory candidate even if the message contains other topics.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states a personal preference, favorite, or like/dislike (e.g., 'my favorite dish is X', 'I love Y'), create a preference memory candidate even if the statement is embedded in a longer message about other topics or follows a question from another participant.
Record the speaker as the subject of the preference and use the 'preference' memory type; do not require the statement to be repeated or confirmed before extraction.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that an explicit 'my favorite dish is lasagna' statement produced no extraction candidates, so the preference was never stored. This indicates the extraction stage can overlook self-disclosed preferences when they appear in longer conversational turns. The rule generalizes to any explicit first-person preference/favorite/like-dislike statement and applies to future construction runs where such statements appear; it stops at implicit preferences or third-party statements that require inference.

payload.name: Separate General Preference from Specific Event
payload.description: When a message contains both a concrete occurrence (e.g., visited a cafe) and a general statement about a recurring preference or habit (e.g., love to discover new places to eat), create separate candidates rather than merging them.
content: During extraction, if a message contains both a concrete event/occurrence and an explicit general statement about a recurring preference or habit (signaled by phrases like 'love to', 'usually', 'always'), create a separate preference candidate for the general statement and an event/state candidate for the concrete occurrence. Do not let the specific event absorb the general statement.

candidates.solves: The extractor collapsed a speaker's general statement ('love to discover new places to eat') into the specific event (visited a cafe), losing the durable preference. The abstract mechanism is conflating a stated recurring preference with its concrete instance during extraction. This rule applies whenever a message contains both a specific occurrence and an explicit general habit/preference statement; it does not apply to purely one-time, non-recurring statements.

payload.name: Extract explicit subjective feelings as memories
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states a subjective feeling or evaluation about an activity or thing (e.g., 'it's magical'), create a preference or state memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, explicitly monitor for utterances where a speaker states a personal feeling or evaluation about an activity, event, or object, often signaled by evaluative adjectives (magical, amazing, exciting, etc.) or phrases (I love, I enjoy, it makes me feel).

When found, create a preference memory (or state memory if clearly temporary) for that speaker, capturing the object and the stated feeling. Do not skip these statements even when embedded in longer supportive or motivational messages.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that an explicit self-report of a feeling (Gina describing dance as 'magical') generated no memory candidate. The abstract mechanism is that subjective evaluative utterances are often skipped during extraction. This skill applies to any future session where a speaker explicitly characterizes an experience or object with an evaluative adjective or phrase, ensuring such statements are stored as durable preference/state memories. It does not apply to purely factual statements or unsupported opinions.

payload.name: Extract explicit key principles as preferences
payload.description: When a conversation message explicitly states a person's key principle, value, or strategy about their work or customers, extract it as a preference memory during construction.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit belief or value statements as preference candidates, even if phrased as encouragement or general advice.
Record the speaker, the belief/value expressed, and the source message; do not require an associated event or plan before extracting.
Do not extend this rule to implied or inferred opinions; the statement must explicitly articulate the principle.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an explicit statement of a speaker's key principle (e.g., that creating a special experience is what makes customers feel welcome) generated no extraction candidate and was never stored. The reusable mechanism is to capture such explicit belief/principle statements as preference memories during extraction. This applies to future conversations where participants state a value or strategy; it does not apply to inferred attitudes or unstated implications.

payload.name: Preserve region for location memories
payload.description: When a message mentions a city, town, or landmark, include its unambiguous state/province/country during extraction and when enriching location memories.
content: When extracting a memory from a message that names a city, town, or landmark, also record the containing state/province/country if that relation is well-known and unambiguous.
When updating or enriching an existing location memory, ensure the broader administrative region is preserved alongside the specific place.
Do not guess ambiguous region mappings; only add the state/province/country when the connection is certain.

candidates.solves: When a conversational message names a city, town, or landmark, extraction often records only that specific place and drops the containing state/province/country, so later state-level or country-level questions cannot be answered from memory. This skill ensures the broader administrative region is preserved whenever it is an unambiguous, well-known fact.

payload.name: Resolve relative vacation times and locations
payload.description: When a message describes a trip, vacation, or photo with a relative time like 'last summer' and a place, resolve the time from the message/session timestamp and extract the visit as an event with a location.
content: During extraction, if a message mentions travel, vacation, or a photo taken on a trip with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last summer', 'last winter', 'a few months ago') and a place, do not skip it for lacking an explicit date.
Resolve the relative time using the message/session timestamp to determine the concrete season or period, and infer the country when the mentioned city is unambiguous.
Create an event memory for the person's visit to that location during the resolved time, linked to the source message, including the specific place name and country when inferable.

candidates.solves: Construction often misses durable facts when a user mentions a vacation or photo with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last summer') and a city, but no explicit date or country. The diagnosed cause was that no candidate was generated from such a message, leaving the place and time unrecorded. This rule applies whenever extraction must resolve relative time from the message timestamp and create a dated location event.

operations.name: Extract each explicitly stated goal as a distinct memory
operations.description: When a speaker explicitly states one or more goals, priorities, or aspirations, extract each as its own memory candidate, including superlative primary goals.
content: During extraction, create a separate candidate memory for each explicitly stated goal or aspiration (e.g., 'my goal is', 'I want to', 'number one goal', 'also want'), even when multiple appear in the same message or turn.
Do not merge multiple distinct goals into one broader memory; keep each goal independently so that downstream reference claims can be matched.

Treat emphatic or superlative goal statements ('my number one goal', 'most important goal') as ordinary explicit goals and extract them even if another goal was already captured from an earlier exchange.

operations.name: Preserve distinct events during memory updates
operations.description: When updating or merging an existing memory, if the new message describes a different event, activity, plan, or instance (different ordinal, date, or topic), do not overwrite the existing memory; ADD a new memory or merge while preserving all prior non-contradicted facts.
content: Before applying UPDATE or MERGE, compare the new message's event/activity/plan with the existing memory's content. If they describe different instances (different ordinal, date/time, completion status, or topic), do not overwrite the existing memory; ADD a new memory for the new instance and leave the old memory unchanged.

When new information enriches the same event instance, preserve all previously stored facts that are not explicitly contradicted; merge new details into the existing content instead of replacing the whole memory.

If a MERGE combines a candidate with an existing memory, ensure every distinct fact from the candidate (e.g., new activity, donation recipient, date) appears in the merged content; if it cannot be retained without losing other key facts, create a separate memory for that fact.
Do not change world_start or other temporal fields during enrichment unless the new message explicitly revises the date of the same event; preserve original dates and details.

operations.name: Preserve original facts when merging or updating related memories

If the incoming information describes a different time period or event kind than the existing memory, create a new memory instead of changing the existing one's kind or world_start.
